3f68700058db28da: HANOI, Oct 5 — Vietnamese police have arrested 12 men accused of stealing nearly 2,700 cats during night raids into residential neighbourhoods, taking the pets to be slaughtered for food, police and state media said today.
Fur removal machines, cat traps and measuring scales were among items confiscated during investigations into the alleged cat-stealing ring in Ho Chi Minh City.
Consumption of dogs and cats is legal in Vietnam, where many restaurants openly advertise the meat, but vendors are required to obtain certificates showing the origin of the animals.
Media reports have said that stolen cats can be sold at restaurants for at least 70,000 dong (US$2.70) per kilogram.
The 12 men were arrested on allegations of property theft and admitted “to stealing and trafficking approximately 2,700 cats of various types”, police said in a statement.
Criminal proceedings began yesterday but it was not clear when the men were detained.
The suspects pounced between 11 pm and 4 am, roaming residential areas on motorbikes in small groups to steal local cats, state media said.
The network was first discovered in July, with police seizing 50 live cats alongside 55 cat traps, two scales and two fur removal machines.
Each team was estimated to have stolen between four and 10 cats per night.
Police in Ho Chi Minh City arrested 18 people earlier this year accused of being part of two separate cat-stealing rings. — AFP
2545b810f6c81373: KUALA LUMPUR: Federal Land Development Authority's (Felda) long-term survival hinges on a fundamental policy decision.
Felda's responsibilities must clearly be redefined so it can operate as a financially sustainable organisation without being continually burdened with wider political and social obligations.

That is the central challenge facing the government as it works on a new strategic direction for Felda following the release of the agency's 2019 White Paper and FGV Holdings Bhd's delisting from Bursa Malaysia.
The issue is not simply whether Felda can generate enough income, but whether it can become financially independent while continuing to meet its obligations to settlers and successive generations.

It is learnt that the thrust of the argument in Felda's new strategic review is: If the commercial decisions determining its financial sustainability are always driven by political decisions, then it will never achieve financial sustainability and independence.
Felda's future model therefore needs a clear definition of what falls within its commercial mandate and what the government or other ministries should bear.
The agency was created with a specific social and economic purpose, but that mandate has expanded over the decades as new generations of settlers emerged and expectations grew.
Felda is now expected to manage plantations, support settlers, provide housing and address the needs of their children and grandchildren, while also remaining financially viable.
The question is where that responsibility ends.
If 95 per cent of the original issues have been settled, there is still the remaining five per cent that Felda has to deal with.
But after that, Felda must be allowed to concentrate on its core business - running and improving its plantation operations.
That includes consolidating and professionally managing about 330,000 hectares of commercial plantation land so the assets can generate sustainable returns.
The land, including some 470,000 hectares owned by its 112,683 settlers, remains a major source of value.
Under a potential long-term leasing model, settlers could retain ownership of their land while professional management improves productivity and generates income from the asset.
However, that model will only work if the underlying land-management problem is resolved.
Fragmentation Threatens Plantation Efficiency
One of the biggest structural challenges is fragmentation.
Felda settlers were originally allocated sizeable plots, but introducing individual titles and subsequent inheritance have progressively complicated land management.
A plantation cannot be managed efficiently if one plot is replanted while another is not, or if individual owners make different decisions on fertiliser, harvesting and replanting.
An estate works because activities can be coordinated across large areas, creating economies of scale in procurement, planting, harvesting and logistics.
Fragmented holdings undermine those efficiencies.
The problem is particularly serious when replanting is required.
A plantation operator must spend heavily before new trees begin producing meaningful income.
For Felda, replanting to replace old trees is estimated to cost about RM36,000 per hectare.
Felda must also continue supporting settlers during that period, making replanting both a financial and social burden.
The proposed new model needs to create an operating structure capable of managing land as a commercial plantation while protecting the economic interests of settlers.
That could involve longer-term leasing arrangements, professional estate management and a greater role for cooperatives.
But ownership, management and income distribution must be clearly separated.
The issue is further complicated by succession.
The original settler generation has aged, while land has passed to children and grandchildren.
The community now extends across multiple generations, with estimates of the wider Felda population running into millions.
The danger is that continued subdivision of land could eventually make individual holdings economically unviable.
The policy question, therefore, is not whether Felda should continue supporting its community, but what form that support should take and who should pay for it.
If the government wants Felda to remain financially independent, it cannot indefinitely expand the agency's scope of responsibility.
Housing for the next generation may be a legitimate government policy objective, but it does not necessarily have to be funded indefinitely through Felda's balance sheet.
Similarly, education, health, rural development and other social programmes fall within the responsibilities of other ministries and agencies.
These obligations should be better allocated rather than automatically placed on Felda.
Legal Reform To Redefine Mandate
To redefine its responsibilities effectively, Felda requires a review of the legal framework governing the agency and its land-management structure.

This will require amendments to the three key laws that shape Felda's operations: the Group Settlement Areas Act 1960, the Federal Land Consolidation and Rehabilitation Authority Act 1966 (commonly known as the Felda Act), and the National Land Code 1965.
The Group Settlement Areas Act should be reviewed to address the realities of fragmented ownership, succession and the coordinated management of plantation land.
Any amendments must preserve settlers' ownership rights while allowing land to be managed collectively and professionally where this is necessary to protect productivity and long-term income.

The Felda Act should also be amended to provide a clearer distinction between Felda's commercial responsibilities and the social or developmental functions that the government or other public agencies should fund.
The act should define Felda's mandate more precisely, including its role in managing plantation assets, supporting settlers and pursuing commercial investments.
It should also provide greater clarity on Felda's authority to enter into long-term leasing, management and restructuring arrangements while ensuring accountability and protection for settlers.

The National Land Code must likewise be examined because land administration, titles, transfers, inheritance and restrictions on dealings directly affect Felda's ability to manage plantation areas as viable commercial estates.

Without changes to the land framework, efforts to consolidate fragmented holdings or introduce coordinated management may remain difficult, particularly where ownership is divided among multiple heirs.
The three laws must therefore be reviewed together rather than amended in isolation.
Amending one act without corresponding amendments to the others could create further legal uncertainty and limit Felda's ability to implement a coherent operating model.
The objective should not be to weaken settlers' rights, but to ensure that those rights can be protected within a financially sustainable plantation structure.
Any legislative amendments should be accompanied by clear safeguards on ownership, compensation, income distribution, consent, dispute resolution and accountability.
The government must also consult settlers, their representatives, state authorities and other stakeholders before finalising the proposed changes.
Ultimately, Felda cannot be expected to operate under a modern commercial model while being governed by laws designed for an earlier phase of land settlement and rural development.
Legal reform is therefore a necessary part of redefining Felda's responsibilities and creating a clearer division between commercial operations and public policy obligations.
FGV Delisting: Part Solution, Part Problem
The delisting of FGV is another important part of the restructuring.
FGV was officially delisted from Bursa Malaysia on Aug 28, 2025, returning the plantation group to private ownership under Felda.
The move was intended to give the group greater flexibility and align it more closely with Felda's long-term objectives.
But delisting does not, by itself, solve Felda's structural problems.
The agency must still address the financial and governance issues highlighted in the 2019 White Paper, including questions surrounding eight investments and transactions.
One recommendation from the review is for Felda to focus on its core assets and dispose of non-core assets where doing so makes commercial sense.
Assets that do not contribute to the plantation and agribusiness core should not continue consuming management attention and capital.
However, some non-core assets are difficult to sell because they have fallen in value or involve unresolved legal, financial or governance issues.
Examples include investments and properties acquired during FGV's expansion after its 2012 listing.
The strategy of buying assets during the post-listing period created a diversified portfolio, but it also left FGV and Felda with investments that are now difficult to monetise.
Such assets should be subjected to proper forensic and commercial assessments.
If an asset has no strategic value and can be sold at a reasonable price, it should be considered for disposal.
But if an investment is already impaired, selling it at a large loss may not necessarily solve the underlying problem.
The more difficult cases involve investments where substantial amounts have already been spent but recovery prospects remain uncertain.
It is understood that the Indonesian Eagle High investment is among examples cited in the discussion about Felda's new strategic direction.
The question is whether Felda should continue waiting for recovery from such investments or recognise that some capital may never be recovered.
Past investments cannot simply be carried indefinitely on the balance sheet because no one is willing to make the difficult decision to recognise the loss.
At the same time, the government cannot expect every problematic asset to be disposed of immediately if doing so would destroy further value.
The answer is to distinguish between commercially recoverable assets, assets that can be restructured and assets where recovery has effectively been exhausted.
Only then can Felda establish a realistic starting point for its next phase.
The real test is financial independence
The ultimate objective should be a Felda that can fund its core operations, including replanting and estate management, from sustainable commercial returns.
That requires stronger plantation productivity, better procurement, economies of scale and disciplined capital allocation.
It also requires a clear separation between Felda's commercial role and the government's wider social responsibilities.
The agency cannot be expected to become financially independent while simultaneously being asked to finance an expanding list of obligations.
32a03143604804e4: TAIPING: The bodies of the four people killed in a three-vehicle crash on the East-West Highway in Gerik yesterday were released to their families today after post-mortem examinations at Taiping Hospital.
The first body, that of Al Zubair Deraman, 31, was taken out of the hospital's forensic unit at 9.55am.
It was followed by the body of Mohamad Hafiz Daniel Nik Hairey, 19, at 12.30pm.
The bodies of Tuan Shazrin Tuan Mud, 40, and her 3-year-old daughter were taken out of the mortuary at 1.32pm.
The victims' relatives were understood to have arrived from Kelantan as early as 8am.
They were later expected to take the bodies to Kota Baru for burial.
The 3-year-old girl's identity has yet to be officially confirmed.
The crash also left Tuan Shazrin's other child, Mohammad Shiraz Hammani Abdul Fattah, 9, critically injured.
He remains warded at Taiping Hospital.
Meanwhile, Hafiz Daniel's uncle, Mohd Yasri Yasim, 43, said the group had been returning to Kelantan after a fishing trip in Gerik when the crash occurred.

"Based on what I know, Hafiz Daniel will be buried in Kampung Tok Jawa in Pawang, Bachok," he said.
The crash involved three vehicles and claimed four lives on the East-West Highway yesterday.

1abad39230e2a326: KUCHING, Oct 5 — Sarawakian statesman Datuk Song Swee Guan has been remembered as a selfless and caring man who was able to balance between work and family.
Grieving family members remember the former assemblyman, MP, State Legislative Assembly (DUN) Speaker, and Kuching South’s first mayor as someone who quietly sacrificed so much for others.
According to Song’s niece Kaylene Tan, his dedication to his work and selfless care for his parents kept him single.

“I believe he was a very good son. My grandfather – his father – was bedridden for many years and he would look after him, especially when he was unwell at night. When he needed attention at night, my uncle would go there and help him and look after him.

“I was still very little at that time, but what was amazing was that he was able to balance his service to the community in Kuching as well as his parents effortlessly. And he never brought the work home,” she told The Borneo Post at her uncle’s wake.
Tan said when Song was at home, he was fully focused on the family, his parents, cooking, and having a laugh with them.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sarawakian statesman Datuk Song Swee Guan was known to be a good cook by family members. — The Borneo Post pic

“Years later, after my grandfather passed away, my uncle continued caring for my grandmother. He made sure she ate well, that she had company, made sure that she was driven from place to place. So, he was a very good son,” she said.
Reflecting on her uncle’s lesser-known qualities, she revealed that he loved to cook, noting that he cooked delicious chicken curry and kacang ma.
She said Song used to bring her sister, brother, grandmother, and herself for long evening drives around Kuching city.
“He was like a hero. Whenever he stopped at the shops or the wet markets, he said: ‘I don’t want to go out,’ from the car because he would be ‘flooded’ by all these hawkers.
“And that was during his time as the mayor. He was very popular with the people,” she recalled.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Song Chai Kim (left) and her daughter Kaylene Tan (right) share their memories of her brother and Tan’s uncle, the late Datuk Song Swee Guan, at home. — The Borneo Post pic
She also shared that Song loved cats and theorised on the inspiration behind the famous white cat statue in Padungan.
“You know that white cat statue? At the time when it was launched back then, my grandmother had a white cat.
“I’m not so sure if the white cat statue was inspired by the white cat,” Tan said.
Tan’s mother Song Chai Kim remembered how close she and her older brother were.
“Oh, we had a very happy childhood together, played together, did a lot of things together. We were very close.
“He went overseas to study at a very young age, then I got married and I’ve been staying in Singapore since then.
“Despite the distance, we still managed to maintain a close relationship. We were a very close family,” she said.
Song’s foster son Sim Min Min said they often spent time together over coffee.
“We were close. He was like a father figure to me, and he considered me as a son.
“He was a well-mannered man who loved to help people and he would try to help them however he could,” Sim said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sim Min Min recalls time spent over coffee with Sarawakian statesman Datuk Song Swee Guan, whom he described as ‘a father figure’. — The Borneo Post pic
He added for the past 20 years, Song had been an active hiker until he suffered mobility issues.
Song was appointed a councillor of the Kuching Municipal Council (KMC) in 1981 before becoming its chairman in 1982.
He led the council until 1988 and subsequently became the founding mayor of Kuching South in August that year, following the delineation and establishment of Kuching South.
Song served for four terms as Padungan assemblyman from 1983 to 2001 and as Bandar Kuching MP from 1995 to 2003.
He was also DUN Speaker from 1996 to 2000.
He passed away peacefully on Sunday at 3.30pm at Sarawak General Hospital. — The Borneo Post
* Editor’s note: DUN is an abbreviation in Malay for Dewan Undangan Negeri, or the State Legislative Assembly.
ee456201eb9f2731: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Bar failed in its bid to challenge the appointment of Federal Court judge Tan Sri Ahmad Terrirudin Mohd Salleh to the Judicial Appointments Commission (JAC).
High Court judge Norliza Othman dismissed the Bar's application for leave to initiate judicial review proceedings, finding that its proposed challenge was not arguable in law.

She ruled that Section 5(1)(e) of the Judicial Appointments Commission Act was clear and required only that the appointee be a serving Federal Court judge and that the appointment be made by the Prime Minister.
The court found that both requirements had been fulfilled in Ahmad Terrirudin's appointment.

Norliza said the Bar was asking the court to read additional requirements into the provision, including seniority, length of service, previous High Court or Court of Appeal experience, freedom from unresolved allegations, consultation and compliance with an asserted convention.
However, none of those requirements appeared in the Act.
"The provision requires only a serving Federal Court judge appointed by the Prime Minister.
"Both are satisfied, and the court cannot read in criteria Parliament did not enact," she said.
The court also rejected the Bar's arguments that the appointment was illegal and irrational, ruling that it was made in accordance with the law.
On irrationality, the court found that nothing in the appointment was so illogical or contrary to accepted moral standards that no sensible decision-maker could have reached it.
"Suspicion and unresolved allegations cannot found review," she said.

On locus standi, the court said there was "considerable force" in the Attorney-General's submission that the Malaysian Bar was not adversely affected within the meaning of Order 53 Rule 2(4) of the Rules of Court.

It said the JAC merely recommends candidates for judicial appointment, while the power of appointment lies with the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on the advice of the Prime Minister under Article 122B of the Federal Constitution.
The court described the alleged fear of bias arising from one member of the nine-member commission as "remote, indirect and speculative".
"Reform, if desired, lies with Parliament. Our function is to interpret the words used, not to supply the words omitted," it said.
The Malaysian Bar filed the leave application on Feb 12, naming Ahmad Terrirudin, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, the JAC and the government as respondents.
The Bar is seeking a certiorari order, which would cancel Anwar's decision to appoint Ahmad Terrirudin as a JAC member.
It is also asking the court to order Anwar to exercise his power to appoint JAC members in accordance with Malaysian law, constitutional conventions and the JAC Act.
The Bar further seeks a mandamus order directing the establishment of a royal commission of inquiry to investigate allegations against Ahmad Terrirudin, with the findings to be made public.
It is also asking the court to declare the appointment unlawful, null and void, and to suspend it pending the disposal of the judicial review proceedings.
According to a Federal Government Gazette dated Nov 18 last year, Ahmad Terrirudin was appointed as a JAC member for a two-year term from Nov 15, 2025, to Nov 14, 2027.

7a1a1472115e1a86: KRYVYI Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees.

Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the sprawling industrial city — which stretches along the banks of the Inhulets River — was doing everything possible to ensure its hospitals remain open, the lights remain on in kindergartens and schools, and buses keep running.
"In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, 52, a former mining executive, said in a video address.
The financial squeeze on the city of about 600,000 people underlines the challenges facing Ukraine as the government navigates its biggest budget crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Last month, the city's largest employer — ArcelorMittal's hulking mining and steelmaking complex — suspended its operations following a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes that darkened its furnaces.
The prospects for next year, Vilkul said, are bleak.
"It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," he said.

It's a scene played out across Ukraine's once-mighty steel industry, which accounted for a tenth of economic output before the war. Giant mills in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast and other industrial cities stand silent and exports have stopped.

An escalation in Russia's drone and missile strikes this summer destroyed factories and warehouses across Ukraine, damaged ports and railways, and forced shops and businesses to close, slowing the growth of the economy and tax revenue.
Meanwhile, the technology-driven war is becoming ever more expensive for Ukraine to fight.

Billions of euros in foreign loans have been delayed by failure to pass bills including unpopular tax reforms and anti-corruption legislation demanded by Ukraine's Western allies, leaving a gaping hole in state coffers.
Ukraine needs US$56 billion to fund that gap this year —equivalent to about a quarter of its economic output. Of that, US$27 billion is military spending.
To bridge the shortfall, Ukrainian officials met European partners in Brussels last week to discuss bringing forward disbursements due next year under a €90-billion (US$101-billion) EU loan.
The European Commission and Ukraine said they had identified funds to close the gap this year.

But three sources familiar with the talks said accelerating these payments risked increasing budget pressure next year - at a time when looming election campaigns in European allies including France and Poland could erode support for Kyiv.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi acknowledges the situation is "challenging." The government has been forced to freeze non-essential spending — including reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure — to prioritise military spending, public sector wages and pensions.
"All resources should be channelled into critically important areas," Koretskyi told reporters.

Two years ago, a single day of fighting cost Ukraine US$140 million, but that figure has jumped to US$190 million, according to Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of parliament's budget committee. And that does not include direct military support to Kyiv from its Western allies.

Rising costs are driven partly by the need for expensive medium- and long-range weapons capable of striking Russia's oil refineries and military factories to reduce Moscow's ability to continue its war.
Plus, the wage bill for an expanded army is higher than ever before, and the state must support a growing number of military families of disabled or deceased soldiers.
"Expenditure will continue to rise," Pidlasa told a conference in Kyiv. "This is one more pragmatic reason why the US and Europe need to act faster to force (Russia) to end this war."
In the first nine months of this year, Ukraine spent more than US$44 billion on defence alone, data showed. That does not include in-kind military support from allies.
In the same period, the government was able to raise only about US$42 billion in tax revenue as the economy slowed.

Pidlasa said that in the first nine months of this year Ukraine's budget lost over 49.5 billion hryvnias (US$1.1 billion) in tax revenue because of Russian attacks that not only damaged property and goods, but disrupted logistics and shut shops and businesses for hours at a time.
By the end of the year, the cumulative losses could rise to 70 billion hryvnias, the government estimates.

"We have not a temporary but a structural problem with the revenues at the very time when spending really requires resources," said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategies, a Kyiv-based think tank.

Some Ukrainian businesses have started to scale back operations. Others have put capital expenditure on hold as the country braces for a difficult winter. Business sentiment and economic expectations are darkening.
Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, founder of an industrial park in the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, said he had scrapped plans to build three new factories.
"The risks are simply too great right now — both for the business and for the people," he said in a Facebook post.

Ukraine's agricultural sector — its largest source of export revenues — has been particularly hard hit. Russian attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports led to a 36.6% fall in grain exports year-on-year in September.
About US$40 billion in export revenue is at risk this year as a result of the blockade, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
Even with tens of billions of euros in foreign support, Ukraine's economy is expected to grow only between 0.5 per cent and 1.5 per cent this year, economists say — down from 1.8 per cent in 2025.

During more than four years of intense fighting, Ukraine has been able to maintain macroeconomic and financial stability thanks to fiscal support from its Western partners, receiving nearly US$200 billion since Russia's invasion.
But US$29.5 billion in foreign aid is now at risk this year because of delays in passing reforms, Koretskyi said.
The government has postponed about US$900 million of capital spending until December, in the hope the legislation will be passed.
The aim is to pass all the required legislation in parliament by Oct 15, Koretskyi said.
"Only then we will get all the money," Koretskyi said. "This is absolutely vital. It needs to be done as soon as possible."
Legislators are now discussing the budget for next year. The government has proposed record defence budget spending of $110 billion. This figure does not include direct military aid.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded budget gap for the next year is already more than US$32 billion.

Part of the solution, Marchenko said, is to use frozen Russian assets in Europe to fund Ukraine's budget. EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine.
"Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X.

48c619080b41fb7c: KUALA LUMPUR: Mahkamah Tinggi menolak permohonan Badan Peguam mendapatkan kebenaran memulakan prosiding semakan kehakiman untuk mencabar pelantikan Hakim Mahkamah Persekutuan Ahmad Terrirudin Salleh ke Suruhanjaya Pelantikan Kehakiman (SPK).

Badan Peguam seterusnya memohon perintah untuk memaksa Terrirudin menunjukkan sebab serta mengemukakan asas pelantikannya dalam SPK.
Permohonan terbabit menamakan Terrirudin, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim, dan kerajaan sebagai responden pertama hingga ketiga.
Peguam Zainur Zakaria, Ambiga Sreenevasan, dan Steven Thiru mewakili Badan Peguam, manakala Peguam Kanan Persekutuan Shamsul Bolhassan dan Nurhafizza Azizan bertindak bagi pihak peguam negara.

4789db23c86e0308: Most senior infrastructure people could tell you what they would do with their file estate if they were starting again. Far fewer will tell you what they actually did, because the honest version tends to involve a VPN that was meant to be temporary and a NAS that has outlived two migration plans. That honest version is what The Register is after at a dinner in Soho on Tuesday 20 October. Joe Fay of The Register chairs, and Rupert Watson, VP for EMEA at LucidLink, is at the table to answer questions. Everyone else is a peer running distributed teams on storage that was bought for an office. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, so what is said can travel but the name attached to it stays in the room. The useful material is the kind nobody puts in a case study: who turned out to still have VPN access months after leaving, say, or which team quietly set up its own sync service because the official route was too slow, and what the security team said when it found out. The agenda starts where most of those stories end up, with governance and security. How do you keep control of unstructured data once it is spread across offices and home connections, and does the current setup stand up to the threats it now faces? From there the table moves on to cost and performance, including the duplicated storage that piles up when every team keeps its own copy, and to what all of it does for the people who simply need the right file. It is one table and places are limited. Drinks start at 6.30pm at The Soho Hotel on Tuesday 20 October, followed by dinner, with the evening finishing at 9pm. Places go by invitation. Request one here.
568b5b5801f65591: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”

“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.
The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.

On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.

More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.

Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.

According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.
All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI, and at the same time, a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?
It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.

It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?

In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.

With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years.

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it.

I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different.
Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: AI that’s clear about what it can and can’t do and, crucially, that’s not posturing as if it’s about to take over the world.

4b3e53d6def2de9d: MADRID: Spanish prime minister Pedro Sanchez said Monday he would call an early election on Nov 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
The defeat in parliament on Friday was another political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the political left still in power.

"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.
His government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.
The defeat infuriated those protesting the country's increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.
Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez's government, for several years.

The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.
Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the EU.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90%, according to real estate website Idealista.
Abascal's eviction catalysed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.

The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275%, say housing campaigners.
The backlash led the property's new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.

The housing bills Sanchez's leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts – on whose support the government relies – voted against them, arguing they lacked rigour.

0f38064548447387: PARIS, Oct 5 — Sixteen years after being portrayed as a power-hungry start-upper in The Social Network film, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg is set for another damning on-screen depiction, this time as a ruthless Silicon Valley overlord.

Hitting screens internationally from Wednesday, the follow-up movie The Social Reckoning by Aaron Sorkin delves into the darkest corners of Facebook’s legacy, from spreading hate speech to encouraging political polarisation, and undermining democracy.

It is told through the real-life story of Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, played by Anora star Mikey Madison, and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), who were the duo behind the 2021 “Facebook Files” PR disaster for the company.
The Zuckerberg character, played by Succession star Jeremy Strong, is the central figure in the drama, but the heroic Haugen and hard-working Horwitz provide the emotional core of the film.
“This is a whistleblower story. It’s a newspaper story,” Sorkin told AFP and a handful of other entertainment journalists last week.

“In The Social Network I made an attempt to understand his (Zuckerberg’s) motives and get inside his head. I do that less in The Social Reckoning,” added Sorkin, who wrote the script of the first movie.
“I put him in a single situation and have him make a single argument so that by the end of the film he is confronted with the consequences of what he’s done,” Sorkin said.

That situation is Facebook’s refusal to fact-check political advertisements on its platform in the run-up to the 2020 US elections, which ended with President Donald Trump contesting the results and his supporters smashing their way into the Capitol.
Cool kids
Critically acclaimed The Social Network in 2010, which went on to win three Oscars, was written by Sorkin but directed by Fight Club maker David Fincher.

It featured a break-out performance from Jesse Eisenberg as a then-student Zuckerberg, a socially awkward mogul-in-the-making who has trouble making friends and is accused of ripping off the idea for Facebook from his peers at Harvard University.

“What I had suggested back in 2010 was that he was a guy uncomfortable with the social structure of college — feeling, as so many people do, that there’s a cool kids table somewhere and he’s not welcome at it,” Sorkin said.
“And so he created his own cool kids table, which he’s now the mayor of.”

In The Social Reckoning, Sorkin does not wrestle with what motivates 42-year-old Zuckerberg as he runs his Meta empire that now includes Instagram, WhatsApp and his faltering parallel online world called the “Metaverse”.
“It can’t possibly be money. There’s nothing you can buy for us$120 billion that you couldn’t buy for us$119 billion,” Sorkin said.
Jeremy Strong told GQ magazine last month that he had reached out to the Meta supremo via email to say he had approached the role “very seriously” and “with respect”.
He did not reveal Zuckerberg’s response.
On screen, the Zuckerberg character is heard acknowledging his image problem, saying: “I know what people think of me”.
‘Tech bros’ on screen
The American tech billionaire class is inspiring a growing number of films, while also becoming more tightly enmeshed in the business side of Hollywood.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was set to be the subject of new biopic Artificial by Italian director Luca Guadagnino until it was dropped by producers Amazon MGM Studios — shortly after Amazon entered into a partnership with OpenAI.
Independent film distributor Neon has stepped in and is set to release the movie next year.

Elon Musk was seen as inspiration for the space-faring main character in black comedy Mickey 17 starring Robert Pattinson last year, while the Tesla and SpaceX boss is the subject of a new documentary by Oscar winner Alex Gibney.
British comedy writer-turned director Jesse Armstrong made Mountainhead for HBO last year that imagined four tech billionaire villains stuck in a mountain retreat.
Given the deep pockets and powerful lawyers available to Zuckerberg, Sorkin’s script was picked over at studio Sony Pictures’ behest.
The West Wing creator also re-shot two scenes, but has denied legal fears were to blame.
“Under normal circumstances when you’re doing non-fiction, there is a thorough legal vet that happens. In this case, they decided to hire an outside law firm just to handle this,” Sorkin explained.
“There were some, not many notes from the lawyers and those notes did not affect (the film),” he said. — AFP
69ef6303aca99460: YANGON, Oct 5 — Myanmar has repatriated nearly 10,000 migrants from Malaysia this year, state media said on Monday, a day after a flotilla returning almost 1,500 of its citizens docked in the country.
The United Nations (UN) has sharply criticised Malaysia’s push to return migrants to Myanmar under an opaque scheme it says cannot guarantee safe homecomings to the war-torn nation.
A group of 1,476 returnees arrived by ship outside Yangon on Sunday, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid a wave of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Rights monitors have raised concerns that members of the Rohingya minority may be sent back to Myanmar, where they have faced violent persecution, but Malaysia has not commented on the ethnicities of returnees.
Myanmar revealed on Monday that a parallel and larger repatriation push has also been taking place by plane.
Between January and August this year, “8,041 citizens were repatriated by air”, state newspaper The Global New Light of Myanmar said.
While the ship returns have been highly publicised in Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur has not commented on the returns Myanmar says it organised by weekly flights.
The total number of migrants Myanmar has said returned by plane and ship this year is 9,517.
Malaysia insists returnees under its scheme agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centres, where Myanmar says they had “faced difficulties” after serving sentences for immigration offences.
But rights groups report dire conditions in the facilities, and the UN refugee agency says staff were not allowed to verify that decisions to return were “were genuinely free and informed”.
More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed in Myanmar since a military coup in 2021 unleashed civil war, according to monitor organisation ACLED.

The Rohingya started fleeing the country en masse to Malaysia before that, escaping a military crackdown starting in 2017 deemed a genocide by rights groups — a charge the armed forces have always denied.
The Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to UN data, and have been the focus of recent anti-migrant sentiment.
After the ships carrying the 1,476 migrants docked Sunday in Thanlyin, just south of Yangon, AFP journalists saw dozens moved to a monastery holding centre for ID and health checks.

“Necessary arrangements are continuing to facilitate their swift reunion with relatives and family members, ensuring their safe return to their respective hometowns,” The Global New Light of Myanmar said. — AFP
125432d3e88285ab: KUALA LUMPUR: The High Court today dismissed the Malaysian Bar’s application for leave to commence judicial review proceedings to challenge the appointment of Federal Court judge Ahmad Terrirudin Salleh to the Judicial Appointments Commission.
In delivering her decision, Justice Norliza Othman held that Section 5(1)(e) of the JAC Act 2009 was unambiguous.
“Section 5(1)(e) is plain. It specifies the category of person: a Federal Court judge; and the appointing authority: the prime minister, and stops there,” she said.

Since both conditions were met, she said, the court could not read non-statutory criteria such as seniority, length of service, and freedom from unresolved allegations into the provision, as none of those requirements appeared in the legislation.
The court rejected the Bar’s arguments on illegality and irrationality, stating that unproven allegations and inferences could not form the basis of judicial review.
Norliza also emphasised that the court’s role was to interpret the law as enacted by Parliament.
Terrirudin, a former attorney-general, was elevated to the Federal Court in November 2024.

The Bar, which represents about 24,000 lawyers in Peninsular Malaysia, filed the application in February, seeking 11 orders, including a certiorari order to quash the prime minister’s decision to appoint Terrirudin to the JAC on Nov 15 last year.
Terrirudin is to serve as a JAC member for a two-year term, from the date of his appointment until Nov 14, 2027.

The Bar also sought a mandamus order compelling the prime minister to exercise his prerogative to appoint a member to the JAC in accordance with the law, established conventions, and the JAC Act 2009.
It further sought an order compelling Terrirudin to show cause and disclose the basis of his appointment to the JAC.
It named Terrirudin, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and the government as the first to third respondents.
Lawyers Zainur Zakaria, Ambiga Sreenevasan and Steven Thiru represented the Bar, while senior federal counsels Shamsul Bolhassan and Nurhafizza Azizan appeared for the attorney-general.
dffcd58a47bd1f05: KUALA LUMPUR: Kerajaan patut menggubal akta pelarian sendiri bagi menetapkan prinsip, tempoh pengurusan, jalan keluar, dan kebertanggungjawaban menangani isu pelarian.

Madius Tangau (GRS-Tuaran), berkata tanpa akta khusus, pengurusan pelarian terlalu bergantung kepada arahan pentadbiran dan budi bicara yang luas, sekali gus berisiko menjurus ketidakselarasan, salah urus, pertimbangan politik serta salah guna kuasa.
“Kalau Malaysia mahu mengurus pelarian dengan cara Malaysia sendiri, mengapakah kita tidak mahu mempunyai akta pelarian Malaysia?

“Tanpa satu akta jelas, terlalu banyak bergantung pada budi bicara pentadbiran. Budi bicara yang terlalu luas boleh meningkatkan risiko ketidakselarasan, pertimbangan politik tidak terkawal, dan salah guna kuasa,” katanya di Dewan Rakyat.

Madius berkata, kerajaan perlu belajar daripada pengalaman lalu mengurus tiga kelompok pelarian iaitu Vietnam, Filipina di Sabah, dan Rohingya di Semenanjung, sebelum menentukan masa depan Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (DPP).

Katanya, pengalaman pelarian Vietnam menunjukkan perlindungan sementara perlu mempunyai jalan keluar yang jelas, apabila kira-kira 240,000 pelarian Vietnam di negara ini ditempatkan semula ke negara ketiga sejak 1975, manakala kira-kira 9,000 pulang ke negara asal.
Sebaliknya, katanya, isu pelarian Filipina di Sabah berlarutan lebih 50 tahun sehingga kini, termasuk berkaitan dokumentasi dan masalah yang diwarisi generasi berikutnya.
“Status sementara tanpa 'exit policy' boleh menjadi masalah tiga generasi. Oleh itu, DPP jangan menjadi IMM13 ( versi baru,” katanya.
Dokumen IMM13 dikeluarkan kepada warga Filipina yang melarikan diri ke Sabah pada tahun 1970-an dari negara asal mereka di selatan Filipina ekoran krisis politik di wilayah selatan negara itu.

Dalam pada itu, Madius berkata, pendekatan baharu melalui DPP, termasuk pendaftaran oleh kerajaan, data biometrik, dan penentuan status pelarian, perlu disertai jawapan jelas mengenai apa yang berlaku selepas seseorang mendapat dokumen itu.
Katanya, kerajaan juga perlu menjelaskan kriteria diguna bagi menguruskan setiap kelompok pelarian supaya dasar negara tidak dilihat sebagai ad-hoc, dengan pendekatan berbeza bagi setiap krisis.
2f46b67406fdc072: YANGON: Myanmar has repatriated nearly 10,000 migrants from Malaysia this year, state media said on Monday, a day after a flotilla returning almost 1,500 of its citizens docked in the country.
The UN has sharply criticised Malaysia's push to return migrants to Myanmar under an opaque scheme it says cannot guarantee safe homecomings to the war-torn nation.
A group of 1,476 returnees arrived by ship outside Yangon on Sunday, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid a wave of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Rights monitors have raised concerns that members of the Rohingya minority may be sent back to Myanmar, where they have faced violent persecution, but Malaysia has not commented on the ethnicities of returnees.
Myanmar revealed on Monday that a parallel and larger repatriation push has also been taking place by plane.
Between January and August this year, "8,041 citizens were repatriated by air," the state newspaper The Global New Light of Myanmar said.
While the ship returns have been highly publicised in Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur has not commented on the returns Myanmar says it organised by weekly flights.
The total number of migrants Myanmar has said returned by plane and ship this year is 9,517.
Malaysia insists returnees under its scheme agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centres, where Myanmar says they had "faced difficulties" after serving sentences for immigration offences.
But rights groups report dire conditions in the facilities, and the UN refugee agency says staff were not allowed to verify that decisions to return were "genuinely free and informed".
More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed in Myanmar since a military coup in 2021 unleashed civil war, according to monitoring organisation ACLED.

The Rohingya started fleeing the country en masse to Malaysia before that, escaping a military crackdown starting in 2017 deemed a genocide by rights groups – a charge the armed forces have always denied.
The Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to UN data, and have been the focus of recent anti-migrant sentiment.
After the ships carrying the 1,476 migrants docked Sunday in Thanlyin, just south of Yangon, AFP journalists saw dozens moved to a monastery holding centre for ID and health checks.

"Necessary arrangements are continuing to facilitate their swift reunion with relatives and family members, ensuring their safe return to their respective hometowns," The Global New Light of Myanmar said.
2221b1dfe4f7e96f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — The government has managed to reduce its subsidy expenditure by 40.1 per cent to RM23.43 billion in 2025 from RM39.10 billion in 2024, supported by the decline in crude oil prices and the implementation of the targeted diesel and petrol subsidy reforms.

According to the Auditor General’s Report (LKAN) 2/2026 on the Federal Government’s Financial Statements for 2025, the RM15.67 billion reduction was partly attributable to a significant decrease in petroleum product subsidy, from RM34.91 billion in 2024 to RM19.11 billion in 2025.

“The reduction in subsidy expenditure was partly due to the decline in global crude oil prices and initiatives to reform targeted diesel subsidies from June 2024 and petrol subsidies from September 2025,” the report said.
It said the average global crude oil price fell to US69.05perbarrelin2025fromUS80.81 per barrel in 2024.

Petrol subsidy expenditure fell 46.5 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) to RM10.51 billion from RM19.66 billion in 2024, while diesel subsidy expenditure declined 48.2 per cent y-o-y to RM5.98 billion from RM11.54 billion previously.
Meanwhile, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) subsidy expenditure decreased 29.1 per cent y-o-y to RM2.63 billion from RM3.71 billion previously.
At the same time, expenditure on welfare grants and assistance for communities, individuals and families increased 380.8 per cent to RM20.36 billion in 2025 from RM4.24 billion in 2024.

“The increase in expenditure was partly due to the disbursement of Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA), Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR), the Madani Subsidy Assistance Programme (BUDI Madani) and STR operating costs,” the report said. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: LKAN stands for Laporan Ketua Audit Negara (Auditor General’s Report).
0c9bcb02ba54f867: PETALING JAYA: Zetrix AI Bhd says it is in discussions to resolve the suspension of its road transport department (JPJ) services, which took effect today.

3b977cece3c874cc: KUALA LUMPUR: The federal government managed to recover only 5%, or RM465 million, of the RM9.27 billion in outstanding loans in 2025.
“The ineffective collection of loan repayments has necessitated restructuring as a recovery measure to assist borrowers in settling their repayments,” the Auditor-General’s Report 2/2026 said.
It also found fresh arrears amounting to RM16.15 million even after the loans had been restructured up to five times.
The repayment period for the restructured loans was extended by 10 to 40 years.

“As a result, the federal government also lost the potential to recover principal balances amounting to RM127.33 million and had to forgo interest and late-payment interest revenue amounting to RM450.99 million due to write-offs.”
The Auditor-General’s Report recommended that the finance ministry strengthen its monitoring and enforcement mechanisms for loan repayments, including issuing notices.
It also recommended legal action against borrowers who default on their loans without reasonable justification.

“In addition, stricter financial capacity analyses and risk assessments should be carried out before approving the disbursement of new loans or the restructuring of loans in order to curb the government’s exposure to the risk of losses.
“The finance ministry should assess the loan restructuring process to ensure it genuinely helps to restore the borrowers’ cash flow and improves their ability to repay the loans.”
The report stated that the balance of recoverable loans stood at RM49.22 billion as of Dec 31, 2025, compared with RM49.62 billion in 2024, a decrease of RM398 million.
“The interest and late-payment interest balance also decreased by 13.1%, or RM358 million, to RM2.375 billion in 2025 from RM2.733 billion in 2024.
“The reduction in recoverable loans as well as interest and late-payment interest was due to repayments and write-offs,” the report said.
Recoverable loans are those provided by the federal government to six categories of borrowers: companies, state governments, statutory bodies, various agencies, cooperatives, and individuals.
These loans are provided, among other purposes, to finance water supply projects, public housing, and loan repayments.
4ea193a34552ebd8: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Six states received an Unmodified Opinion, while another six received an Unmodified Opinion with an “Other Matters” paragraph; one state received an Unmodified Opinion with both an “Emphasis of Matter” paragraph and an “Other Matters” paragraph.

According to JAN, significant issues were identified, revealing weaknesses in corporate governance compliance that require the attention of management and the State Governments.

54237a07a1f24eae: COLOMBO: The International Monetary Fund said Monday it had reached a preliminary agreement with Sri Lanka that will allow it to access about US$345 million from its US$2.9 billion bailout programme.
The Washington-based lender also warned that higher energy prices, the El Nino climate phenomenon and the Middle East conflict could threaten its economic recovery.
The agreement marks the latest milestone in Sri Lanka's recovery from its worst economic crisis, which culminated in a sovereign default on US$46 billion of external debt in 2022.
The South Asian nation secured a four-year US$2.9 billion IMF rescue package in 2023.

"Sri Lanka's economy has proved remarkably resilient to successive shocks," the IMF said in a statement, noting the economy had recorded 11 consecutive quarters of expansion after contracting 7.3% in 2022.
But the country "continues to face downside risks from uncertainty over the duration and intensity of the Middle East war, global trade policy, and the impact of El Nino", it added.

The IMF also criticised the government's decision earlier this month to reinstate a US$126 million diesel subsidy, saying fuel prices should continue to adjust in line with international markets while protecting vulnerable households.
It said the central bank should be prepared to tighten monetary policy further if higher energy prices trigger a second round of inflation.
Sri Lanka's central bank recently raised interest rates 100 basis points to 8.75% but has resisted calls for further increases, arguing that they could undermine growth.
The latest agreement clears the way for what is expected to be the penultimate disbursement under the programme, which is due to expire in March.
Sri Lankan authorities have yet to decide whether they will seek a new arrangement with the IMF when the programme ends.

90296fcbccad7c29: OCTOBER 5 — Gen Alpha is often described as the screen generation. Born into a world of smartphones, tablets, streaming platforms, artificial intelligence and video games, children today are frequently assumed to spend much of their childhood looking at a screen.
But perhaps that description is too simple.

A 12-year-old boy who came to Malaysia during his summer break offered an unexpected reminder that children growing up in the digital age can still develop remarkably traditional — and highly individual — interests.
His interest is collecting coins, particularly error coins.

For those unfamiliar with the term, an error coin is a coin produced with an unintended mistake during the minting process. The error could involve the design, lettering, date, alignment, metal composition or the way the coin was struck.
While an ordinary coin may have little value beyond its face value, certain genuine and scarce minting errors can become highly sought-after by collectors.
What was particularly fascinating was not simply the collection itself, but the knowledge behind it.
Every coin had a story.

The boy could explain what made a particular coin interesting, identify details that others might overlook and discuss why some errors could make a coin more desirable to collectors. A seemingly ordinary piece of metal suddenly became something worth examining closely.

His collection also carries a sentimental value. A coin album gifted by his grandfather has become a place for preserving the collection, and there is genuine happiness in continuing to add new pieces to it. What began as a hobby has therefore become something that connects generations.

A boy is pictured as the debate continues over whether Gen Alpha is too closely associated with screens and technology. — Pexels pic
More impressive was his willingness to share that knowledge with everyone, regardless of age.

There was no hesitation in explaining the differences between coins or pointing out details that adults might easily miss. The usual assumption that knowledge flows from older people to younger people was quietly turned upside down. In this case, a 12-year-old became the teacher, while adults became the learners.
That experience raises an interesting question: how much do adults really understand about Gen Alpha?
The generation commonly labelled Gen Alpha is growing up surrounded by technology, but being technologically immersed does not necessarily mean being interested only in technology.
Video games, social media, online entertainment and digital devices may be part of their everyday lives, but they do not define every child’s curiosity.
Some may be fascinated by science. Others may enjoy drawing, sports, music, animals, cooking, collecting toys or studying something as specific as the history of coins.
The difference is that technology can now help these interests grow.
For this young collector, technology was not the destination. It was the tool.

Behind the interest is also a supportive family that encourages his curiosity. His parents provide access to the internet so he can research error coins, learn more about his collection and deepen his knowledge rather than simply use technology for entertainment.

A device could be used to search for information, identify an unusual coin or verify findings with other sources. But the fascination itself existed beyond the screen. The real excitement came from holding the coin, examining it and understanding why it was different.
Perhaps this is where the conversation about Gen Alpha needs to become more nuanced.

Adults sometimes see children spending hours with technology and assume that screens have replaced curiosity. Yet curiosity may simply be taking different forms. A child who appears to be absorbed in a digital world may also be researching an unusual hobby, learning independently or developing expertise in an area adults have never considered.
The most interesting hobbies are sometimes the ones that seem unusual to everyone else.
There is also a lesson here about age.
Knowledge does not always arrive with grey hair, qualifications or years of experience. Sometimes it arrives in the form of a 12-year-old explaining why a tiny difference on a coin matters.
Age may determine how long someone has lived, but it does not determine how much someone can teach.
Adults spend considerable time encouraging children to learn from teachers, parents and books. Perhaps there should be equal encouragement for adults to remain humble enough to learn from children.
A summer visit that could have been remembered simply as a school holiday instead became an unexpected lesson in curiosity, passion and the value of looking beyond assumptions.
And that 12-year-old collector?
He is not simply a young boy fascinated by coins.

He is a nephew — and an unexpected teacher who offered a different way of looking at Gen Alpha: not merely as children hooked on screens, but as a generation capable of discovering fascinating worlds of their own.
* The author is an English Language lecturer at the Centre for Foundation Studies in Science, Universiti Malaya, and can be reached at matthuri@um.edu.my

d1f2aa1a552ce4e1: KUALA LUMPUR: An opposition MP today urged the public not to discriminate against refugees because of one bad apple.
Ahmad Marzuk Shaary (PN-Pengkalan Chepa) said refugees who break the law should be investigated and brought to court.

"But we shouldn’t punish an entire community because of one man’s actions. A community should not bear the burden of one man’s sins," he said when debating a parliamentary select committee report on refugee management in Malaysia.
The PAS man said he was against xenophobia as much as he was against crimes committed by refugees.
He also spoke of a tendency to portray the entire Rohingya and refugee communities as criminals.
He said Malaysians should not allow their dissatisfaction with the government’s shortcomings in managing refugees to influence how they treat the community.
"Do not let anger erode our humanity," he added.

In July, it was reported that a wave of political disinformation targeting the Rohingya population in Malaysia had raised alarm among rights groups which said it was fuelling xenophobia and intimidation against the refugee community.
Anti-Rohingya sentiment surged in late May after social media posts accused them of dumping waste from a cattle slaughter during Hari Raya Haji.
The incident sparked an online petition calling for the government to resettle Rohingya refugees in "another country", which garnered nearly half a million signatures before it was removed.
62cbf1a7f8c5c0f6: SHAH ALAM, Oct 5 — The Sessions Court here was informed today that the representation submitted by the former chief executive officer (CEO) of GISB Holdings Sdn Bhd (GISBH) and three former company accountants to drop money laundering charges against them had been rejected.
Following this, Deputy Public Prosecutor (DPP) Mohd Ashrof Adrin, who appeared alongside DPP Muhamad Ehsan Nasarudin, said the prosecution would proceed with the trial.
“I regret to inform the court this morning that the prosecution wishes to state that the representation has been rejected and the prosecution will proceed with the trial.

“We will be calling between 15 and 20 prosecution witnesses, and regarding the trial dates, I believe we will require six to eight days,” he said during case management proceedings before Judge Datin Fatimah Zahari.

The four accused are Nasiruddin Mohd Ali, 67, who faces 77 charges involving more than RM10 million; Hamimah Yakub, 74, facing 95 charges involving RM11.4 million; Asmat @ Asmanira Muhammad Ramly, 46, facing 68 charges involving RM4.7 million; and Mohd Khushairi Osman, 55, facing 91 charges involving nearly RM12 million.

However, lawyer Datuk Rosli Kamaruddin, representing all four accused, informed the court that the defence intends to submit a new representation once the seized assets are officially returned to his clients.
He said the new representation would, among other matters, address the possibility of resolving the case through a compound offer.

“For the record, the previous representation did not address the issue of exploring a compound, so there may be a representation exploring this issue,” said Rosli, who was accompanied by lawyer Muhammad Zaim Rosli.
He also requested the court to fix a case management date to determine the status of the new representation in January 2027.

After hearing submissions from both parties, Fatimah fixed the trial for April 26 to 28, June 28 to 30 and July 6 to 8 next year, while the status of the second representation by all four accused will be heard on Jan 26.

Meanwhile, Rosli also sought the court’s permission for the return of Nasiruddin’s passport to enable him to travel to Mecca. Nasiruddin, who appeared in court in a wheelchair, intends to meet his fourth wife, Ummu Mubaroqah Ashaari, 32, who is scheduled to undergo a Caesarean section this month.

He said Muhammad Saleh Basharahil Hospital in Makkah had advised Nasiruddin to be present to provide consent for his wife’s surgery, as she is now full-term, although the exact date of the procedure has yet to be determined.

Mohd Ashrof Adrin informed the court that the prosecution did not object to the application, subject to the conditions stipulated in the notice of application, including that the passport be returned to the court on or before Nov 10, 2026.
The judge subsequently allowed the application subject to the stipulated conditions.
On Sept 10, 2025, Nasiruddin and the three former company accountants pleaded not guilty at the Shah Alam Sessions Court to money laundering charges brought against them.

The alleged offences were committed at bank branches in Selangor between 2020 and 2024 and involved transactions with various parties, including bank accounts belonging to GISBH Sdn Bhd, GISB Mart Sdn Bhd, GISB Travel and Tours Sdn Bhd and childcare centre companies.
They were charged under Section 4(1)(b) of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (Act 613), punishable under Section 4(1) of the same Act.

If convicted, an offender is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 years and a fine of not less than five times the amount or value of the proceeds of unlawful activity at the time the offence was committed, or RM5 million, whichever is higher. — Bernama
40de3960c489caab: SINGAPORE, Oct 5 — Balancing high on a ladder against the city skyline, Jonathan Goh looks every bit the seasoned street performer.
What most spectators may not realise is that the 30-year-old busker is also the first Singaporean to graduate with an honours degree in Circus Arts, The Straits Times (ST) reported.

According to ST, the National Centre for Circus Arts in London confirmed that Goh completed its three year programme in July 2025, making him a trailblazer in a country where circus studies are virtually unheard of.

“I was like ‘Okay, die die must at least have good results.’ Throughout my studies, most of the time I’m the just pass, average kind of student... But there was a lot of pressure when I went to circus school knowing that I’m the first... If you don’t do well, then what’s the point of being the first?” he told ST.
Goh’s fascination with circus arts began at 11, after watching a fire spinning act.

He dreamt of formal training while still in secondary school but chose to perform full time instead. Then, the Covid-19 pandemic came and disrupted his career, pushing him to take “a leap of faith” by enrolling in London, despite annual overseas fees of about £18,000 (RM97,167).

As co-chairman of Buskers’ Association Singapore, Goh said his income now ranges between S$6,000 (RM19,129) and S$12,000 a month. Not bad for someone who spends his time balancing ladders and juggling rings.
He laughed that the question he hears most often is, “Can earn money, meh?” But once people find out what he actually pockets, the scepticism usually vanishes.

According to Goh, student life was demanding, and to make ends meet he performed at Covent Garden, earning between £200 and £400 a week. He also took his act to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe during summer breaks, while winters saw him return to Singapore to perform instead.

Today, he credits the intensive training with sharpening his skills across disciplines including trapeze, aerial and Chinese pole, teeter board, and juggling. For him, the degree was not just about recognition but about refining a craft that continues to draw audiences.
0ada2d1c76d1e829: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Nearly 40 per cent of the 40,000 metric tonnes of solid waste generated in the country daily consists of food waste, according to Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming.

He said efforts to address the waste issue require the cooperation of all parties through a “whole-of-nation approach” involving both businesses and consumers to collectively change their attitudes and practices.

“This is a form of waste. Food waste is not a crime, but it is a sin. It is a grave sin when edible food is simply thrown away,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.
Nga said this when replying to a question from Datuk Mumtaz Md Nawi (PN-Tumpat) regarding the latest developments in efforts to reduce waste sent to landfills and increase recycling rates.
Meanwhile, he expressed confidence that the ministry would achieve its target of exceeding a 40 per cent recycling rate by the end of this year.

Nga noted that under the “Trash to Cash” recycling programme, the total collection of recyclable materials between January and August exceeded 7.86 million kilogrammes (kg), with a sales value of over RM2.85 million.

“Secondly, the zero-waste community initiative involving the establishment of 17 active zero-waste community centres during the same period has collected over 111,504 kg of recyclable materials,” he said.
Additionally, Nga said a school-based recycling competition involving 1,680 schools successfully collected 4.95 million kilogrammes of recyclable materials, which were sold for RM2.98 million.
“Based on calculations of the total collected from 2018 to last year, we managed to gather nearly 20 million kilogrammes of recyclable items, generating proceeds exceeding RM10.22 million,” he said.

Responding to a supplementary question from Mumtaz regarding the specific controls and enforcement actions implemented by the Ministry of Housing and Local Government concerning cable theft, including penalties imposed on third parties or buyers, he said the Cabinet views the issue seriously.

“We constantly collaborate and engage with the Ministry of Home Affairs, including examining the need to amend relevant laws to ensure harsher penalties are imposed on cable theft offenders in the country.

“There have been several instances where LRT (Light Rail Transit) operations were disrupted due to cable theft by syndicates; therefore, this matter (amending laws for heavier penalties) is crucial to ensuring we continue to safeguard public safety and the well-being of the people,” he said. — Bernama
afbd3dc896f523fc: Every Monday morning The Register kicks off proceedings by asking the same question – “Who, Me?” – the title of the reader-contributed column in which you share your tales of the occasions on which you didn’t quite nail the brief yet somehow found career relief. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Terry” who told us that in the 1970s he worked for a defense-related company. “I needed 100 meters of RG8 50 ohm coax cable, so ordered it from an ‘accredited’ supplier,” he wrote. “What I didn’t notice was that there was an option for ‘partial delivery’." Terry’s order duly arrived, all one meter of it – plus paperwork explaining that the other 99 meters would be along presently, thanks to the partial delivery option. “Needless to say, the one meter was not enough to span the distance between the two laboratories I was trying to link with an RF connection,” Terry wrote. Offering the partial delivery option cost the supplier their accreditation. Terry later learned that a junior employer at the cable supplier was sacked over the matter, after admitting he thought sending one meter of cable was a jolly jape. “I did not think it was a joke at the time,” Terry wrote. Have you made a procurement error that ended up costing you, or your supplier? If so, don’t short-change your fellow readers! Instead, click here to share your story with Who, Me? Our mailbag is a little short on stories, so contributions of any length are very welcome. ®
9bb15aa46cf9a788: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — The government does not yet intend to make registration on the e-Consular system mandatory for Malaysians abroad, said Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan.

He said registration through the digital platform managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs remains voluntary, but Malaysians residing, travelling or studying abroad are highly encouraged to register to facilitate monitoring and welfare matters.
“Not yet (making registration mandatory). We have not yet considered applying to the government to make it mandatory, but we hope that tourists and Malaysians abroad will use this facility.

“This e-Consular application makes it easier for embassies and diplomatic missions to know the whereabouts of our citizens, while also allowing us to contact them in case of any crisis, natural disaster or emergency,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.
He was replying to a supplementary question from Khairil Nizam Khirudin (PN-Jerantut), who wanted to know whether the government plans to make registration on the e-Consular system mandatory.

Earlier, Datuk Seri Sh Mohmed Puzi Sh Ali (BN-Pekan) asked about the government’s measures to tighten the registration system for Malaysians travelling or residing abroad to ensure they can be detected and assisted promptly in the event of a tragedy, disaster or emergency.

Commenting on the MyWorldAlert safety application, which is now integrated with e-Consular, Mohamad said it functions as a rapid communication system based on the Global Positioning System (GPS), capable of delivering important information and alerts immediately during urgent situations.

Meanwhile, in response to a supplementary question from Sh Mohmed Puzi regarding assistance in bringing back citizens stranded abroad, he said the ministry provides consular assistance in terms of family communication and facilitating the process of savings or fundraising.

“We provide various forms of assistance, but we do not fully bear the financial burden. However, cases like pilgrims stranded in Jeddah and Madinah due to being cheated by unauthorised agents who only bought one-way tickets without return tickets, we still help manage (this),” he said.
Commenting on the developments of the flood tragedy in Nepal that occurred on Aug 26, Mohamad said that 54 Malaysians are still categorised as missing or unaccounted for.

“Although the Nepalese government has halted search and rescue (SAR) operations and shifted to the recovery phase, we have not given up and are still in contact with local police to check the registration books at every trekking route post,” he also said.

He added that Wisma Putra, along with various agencies including the Attorney-General’s Chambers, Bank Negara Malaysia and the National Registration Department, is facilitating the affairs of the heirs, especially concerning applications for the release of death certificates with the relevant ministries in Nepal. — Bernama
