ce35899d8ea8c7e8: There is a question that many non-Malays often ask me, and recently even my wife has raised it: why are Najib Razak and Umno still embraced by Malays, from kampung folk to those with tertiary education?
This question resurfaced following Najib’s conditional pardon allowing for house arrest and Umno’s significant victories in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
In this article, I present my theory. Readers may find the issue worthy of a research project, or even a PhD thesis!
Reason one: taxation

Many Malays pay little or no tax. For example, my two children, both university graduates, earn about RM4,000 per month and contribute only a few ringgit in taxes. I, on the other hand, pay a substantial amount in tax, but a high-earning non-Malay friend pays four times more than I do.

Because many Malays do not feel the weight of taxation, corruption involving public funds does not resonate with them. To them, money for the people comes from a Malay-led government. As long as salaries, festive aid and allowances arrive, they are content.
Reason two: government employment

A large proportion of Malays work in government. The civil service and political leadership are overwhelmingly Malay – about 80%. Salaries are paid every month, so even if corruption drains RM40 billion, Malay wages remain unaffected.
People may say the country is drowning in debt due to 1MDB, but salaries still come in. Why then should the Malays worry about corruption?
If salaries were withheld for even one month, Umno would collapse and Najib would be cursed. But as long as salaries and allowances flow, corruption has no impact.
Reason three: lack of awareness

Civil servants and Malay businessmen are rarely told that their wages and development allocations – roads, schools, infrastructure – are funded largely by taxes paid by non-Malays employed outside government.

The plundering of billions through corruption does not strike home because Malays do not feel the burden of national debt. Thus, corrupt leaders chosen by Malays borrow from external sources while siphoning off wealth that rightfully belongs to the people.
Reason four: Islamic education
Whether at school or university, this issue is never taught. Even Islamic education avoids it, focusing instead on moral issues like alcohol, gambling and pork.
There are three aspects of Islam that cause corruption to be accepted or ignored:

Religious education itself: I have reviewed thousands of Friday sermons, and none explains how tax money becomes salaries or development funds. Corruption is treated as a minor sin, distant and irrelevant to ordinary people.

Political sermons: Some religious teachers from political parties justify corruption, claiming it is not punishable under hudud because it is absent from classical fiqh texts. So, stealing RM200 shoes may warrant amputation but embezzling RM40 billion is not mentioned. As a result, corruption is seen as less serious than drinking alcohol, not wearing the headscarf, or failing to vote for an Islamic party.

Preachers from abroad: Some insist that Muslims must vote for Muslim candidates, even if they are weak or immoral, as long as they are Muslim. This is compounded by political parties promising heaven for those who vote for them. Thus, corruption, slander and insults will be tolerated if the party claims to uphold Islam in politics.
Reason five: party benefits
Malays receive benefits – haj trips, kitchen aid, bicycles – from Malay parties. No one ever asks where the money comes from.
At restaurants, Malays check for halal certificates, but when receiving party contributions, they never question the source of funds.
Reason six: the DAP bogeyman

This is the most classic and effective reason: vote for Malay or Islamic parties to prevent DAP from ruling. My wife’s retiree friends recently admitted voting for Umno out of fear that DAP would take over in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
Malays have never compared the number of DAP members convicted of corruption against Malays from Malay parties.

All they care about is blocking DAP from coming to power because it is a party of infidels. Malays believe it is their religious duty as Muslims to prevent DAP from winning, and in doing so, they feel assured of heaven.
With no proper education at schools, universities or mosques about the impact of corruption, Malays will continue to support parties steeped in it.
I believe that until the end of time, Malays will not change but will go on backing corrupt parties in Malaysia.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d80c3899d56a0a87: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — The secondary school in Yong Peng, Johor, where a Form Four female student was allegedly found murdered, is equipped with CCTV cameras, but none were installed at the location where the incident occurred.

Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said the Ministry of Education (MOE) is now upgrading the CCTV facilities and has launched an investigation into the school’s security company to determine whether there were any breaches of standard operating procedures (SOPs).
“The school does have CCTV, but the cameras were not installed at the scene of the crime. That is why I say, beyond the (new installation) phases...

“...any school that already has CCTV, but where the system is non-functional or damaged, should inform us so that we can work together to improve its functionality, ensuring it can capture and record events within the school,” she told a press conference at the Parliament building today.
Elaborating on security measures, Fadhlina said the ministry is also conducting a comprehensive review of the patrol records and duties carried out by the security company on the day of the incident.
She warned that financial penalties or termination of the contract could be imposed if any breaches of the stipulated terms are found.

Meanwhile, she urged the public to stop spreading false information about the incident out of respect for the grieving family of the victim and the underage suspect, who remains under police investigation.
“There have been claims that the victim was dragged from the surau (prayer room) to the hall where the incident occurred, as well as allegations of broken glass in the surau. None of this is true.
“Let us not add to the pain with speculation,” she said.

While extending her condolences to the victim’s family, Fadhlina said the ministry demanded that justice be served in the death of Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, 16, and had fully entrusted the criminal investigation to the Royal Malaysia Police .
“Regarding Irene Sofiya, our responsibility now is clear. The truth must be uncovered, and justice must be served. Justice for Irene Sofiya,” she said.
Irene Sofiya was found dead, with injuries on her body suggesting that she had been murdered, inside the hall of a secondary school in Yong Peng at 5.30pm last Saturday.
The victim was discovered by her grandmother and a friend, who had gone to the school after realising that she had not returned home even though her extra classes had ended. — Bernama
a13ed816e8b8efd7: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — A total of RM68.81 million in contractor advance payments (WPK) involving 24 projects under five ministries remains unrecovered, with 86.7 per cent of the amount outstanding for more than a decade, according to the Auditor-General’s Report (LKAN) 2/2026.
The five ministries involved are the Ministry of Education (KPM), Ministry of Defence (MINDEF), Ministry of Home Affairs (KDN), Ministry of Transport (MOT) and Ministry of Works (KKR).

The audit found that, overall, the management of WPK by the five ministries complied with the prevailing circulars and financial regulations governing eligibility requirements for contractor advance payments.

“However, the outstanding WPK receivables remained a concern, particularly as a significant portion had been outstanding for more than 10 years and involved companies that had either been dissolved or wound up.
“RM59.63 million out of RM68.81 million in WPK receivables outstanding for more than 10 years involved 21 companies,” the report read.

The report stated that five of the companies had been dissolved, involving WPK receivables amounting to RM10.68 million, while 13 companies had been wound up, involving outstanding WPK of RM27.76 million.
Another three companies remained active, with outstanding WPK amounting to RM21.19 million.

The audit noted that the RM10.68 million owed by dissolved companies could not be recovered, while delays in taking follow-up action against companies that had been wound up had also hindered efforts to recover the outstanding amounts.

Among the delayed actions was the submission of the Proof of Debt Form to the Department of Insolvency (MdI), which is necessary to establish the Government’s claim against companies undergoing winding-up proceedings.
Meanwhile, RM9.18 million in WPK receivables had been outstanding for less than five years, involving three companies that remained active.
The audit also uncovered a reporting issue involving RM5.67 million in WPK balances linked to two projects under KPM and MOT.
The amount had not been reported as WPK receivables, resulting in the actual position of outstanding WPK not being accurately reflected.
The audit called on the ministries to take immediate action to strengthen recovery efforts and ensure that the Government’s financial interests are protected.

For companies that had been wound up under KPM and KKR, the ministries were urged to follow up by submitting the Proof of Debt Form to MdI and obtaining the status of dividend distribution to safeguard the Government’s interests.
The audit also recommended that KPM and KDN take immediate action to initiate civil proceedings or issue letters of demand against companies that remain active if there had been a breach of contract.
Such action, it said, was necessary to ensure that statutory provisions relating to limitation periods were complied with and that the prescribed time limits were not exceeded.
For MOT, the audit recommended that WPK receivables be reported immediately once a Termination Notice is issued to a company.
This would ensure that the reported figures accurately reflect the actual outstanding WPK balance that remains to be recovered.

The findings underscore the need for ministries to strengthen monitoring and follow-up action on contractor advance payments, particularly where companies face financial difficulties, winding-up proceedings or termination of contracts, to prevent public funds from remaining outstanding for prolonged periods.

8e6652744b8ea4ca: Egyptologists have long debated whether the earliest pharoahs of the First Dynasty were buried with various servants and officials to serve them in the afterlife—a form of human sacrifice. But there is very little archaeological evidence available, given that many of the earliest Egyptian tombs were plundered and/or hastily excavated. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from tombs in the 1920s and concludes that over one-third show evidence of blunt force trauma. This suggests that they may have been victims of so-called "retainer sacrifice."

Author Roselyn Campbell is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue University who has long been fascinated with the history of human sacrifice. "I'm interested in how we as human beings decide which types of violence are okay and which are not, and how we even define violence," Campbell told Ars. "It's very context specific. We have to be careful not to extend our own ideas about what violence is and how it's used into other cultures. With Egypt, we have such a long history of European and colonial archeology; they came in with very specific ideas about what this culture was. You really have to make an effort to contextualize the legacy data we have."

Naturally she found the debate over whether ancient Egyptians practiced retainer sacrifice pertinent to her interests. "People tend to fall into one of two camps," said Campbell. "Either retainer sacrifice definitely happened, end of discussion, or it definitely didn't happen, end of discussion. But nobody's actually looked at the bones in a very long time." Forensic science has advanced considerably over the last century, so re-analysis could be useful. Complicating matters is the fact that older sets of remains are often incomplete and/or modified for preservation, destroying vital forensic information in the process.

0781612f314778e8: Back in 2024, I wrote a column lamenting Bursa Malaysia's decision to keep bitcoin and other crypto assets off its new multi-asset exchange, asking whether it might go down as Bursa's biggest blunder.

Two Thursday's ago, I spent the better part of a day at M Resort & Hotel in Kuala Lumpur listening to regulators, bankers and fund managers talk about digital assets not as a fringe curiosity, but as the plumbing for the next generation of our capital market. What a difference two years makes.

The event was LIDAC26, the Luno Institutional Digital Asset Conference, now in its second edition. Luno, one of the digital asset exchanges registered with the Securities Commission Malaysia (SC), pitched it squarely at institutions rather than retail punters, and the room reflected that.

The main hall kept the headline sessions flowing from 9.30am, four breakout sessions ran in smaller rooms alongside it through the day, and the session screens I saw all carried a QR code for live audience questions.

Attendees could even earn seven continuing professional development (CPD) points, the credits licensed finance professionals collect to keep their qualifications current, which tells you exactly who the organisers were courting.
So what were the big takeaways? Three stood out.
1. Stablecoins are the real story

Luno chief executive James Lanigan opened proceedings with a slide that cut through a lot of the noise. By Luno's count, about RM1.43 trillion worth of assets had been tokenised, or recorded as digital tokens on a blockchain, by the first quarter of 2026, and roughly RM1.26 trillion of that was stablecoins, tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar.

That's right. Around 90% of all tokenised assets are, in effect, digital cash, the overwhelming majority of which is tokenised USD, cementing it as not only the world’s reserve currency but the currency of choice in the budding crypto economy.

Lanigan's framing was that the industry had moved from speculation, through building infrastructure, and was now firmly in its institutional era, with one of his final slides declaring that Malaysia was not a late market, but an early one.
2. The regulator wants substance, not buzzwords
The most anticipated session was that by Wong Huei Ching, the SC's executive director of digital strategy and innovation, who laid out where Malaysia's rules are heading.
Her message, stripped to its core, was that putting an asset on a blockchain is not innovation in itself, and that pilots need to prove their worth before the rules are rewritten.

The SC is practising what it preaches. In April, it teamed up with Khazanah Nasional, our sovereign wealth fund, to price Malaysia's first tokenised sukuk (an Islamic bond recorded on a blockchain), a RM100 million pilot that SC chairman Mohammad Faiz Azmi said would test tokenisation's potential "in a controlled and credible manner".

The market she regulates is growing fast, too. Trading value on Malaysia's licensed digital asset exchanges hit RM17.14 billion in 2025, a 23% jump from RM13.93 billion the year before, according to the SC.
3. The ringgit is going on-chain

John Ho, head of legal and financial markets at Standard Chartered, walked participants in the main hall through Bank Negara Malaysia's growing list of experiments. These include Project Mawar, which explores a wholesale digital ringgit for banks, and the central bank's Digital Asset Innovation Hub, where Standard Chartered and Capital A are testing a ringgit stablecoin, while Maybank trials tokenised deposits.
The prize is not small. One industry estimate cited on stage, and widely reported, puts Malaysia’s tokenisation opportunity at around RM175 billion by 2030.
The tidbits

Many other speakers added flair and colour to the proceedings. Former deputy international trade and industry minister Ong Kian Ming spoke on navigating digital assets in a fragmenting global order, while Harjit Singh of HSS Advisory and Anil Puri of EY tackled a question plenty of Malaysian crypto investors have been asking for years: how exactly will all this be taxed?

My favourite, though, was a breakout billed as Malaysian builders shaping the global digital asset landscape. On one stage sat TM Lee, co-founder of CoinGecko, Matthew Tan, founder of Etherscan, and Siong Ong, co-founder of Jupiter, products used by crypto traders the world over.
CoinGecko and Etherscan were both born right here in Kuala Lumpur, and I can’t help but feel proud that some of the most widely used tools in the industry were built by Malaysians.
Siong Ong’s speaker photo on the big screen? A Pudgy Penguin, an uber popular non-fungible token (NFT) collection. In a day full of suits, it was a welcome reminder of where this industry came from.
The one glaring miss

I was, however, surprised that bitcoin, the 800-pound gorilla in the room, barely got a look-in. Bitcoin alone is worth around RM6.9 trillion today, according to CoinGecko, and together with ether, the Ethereum network's native token, the pair make up about two-thirds of the entire crypto market.

Stablecoins, for all the stage time they got, account for a mere 10%. Despite more than a decade of relentless innovation in the industry, bitcoin still commands over half of all crypto value, and not telling that story was a missed opportunity.

So where does that leave us? The SC revised its guidelines on Mar 2 to permit digital currency exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and Bursa, the very exchange that shut crypto out of its multi-asset platform in 2024, said in March that it welcomed the listing of digital currency ETFs, and told reporters in July that it planned to add them to its line-up.

The regulator has built the framework, Khazanah has shown the plumbing can work and Bank Negara is already testing the ringgit on-chain. All that's left is for the first digital currency ETF to actually start trading on Bursa. After all, it's about time the exchange that once said no had something to show for its yes.

6265a3e1eeb1bec9: Ada dua misteri yang ramai orang bukan Melayu selalu bertanyakan kepada saya dan baru-baru ini, isteri saya pun bertanyakan soalan yang sama. Soalannya adalah kenapa Najib Razak dan Umno masih diterima orang-orang Melayu dari orang kampung sampai ke peringkat pengajian tertinggi?
Soalan ini susulan isu Najib diberi pengampunan dan tahanan rumah serta kemenangan besar Umno di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.
Dalam artikel ini saya kemukakan teori saya yang mungkin ada di kalangan pembaca yang nak buatkan ia sebagai projek penyelidikan atau tesis PhD.

Sebab pertama, saya jelaskan, adalah ramai orang Melayu tidak membayar cukai atau pun bayarannya sedikit sahaja. Ramai pekerja Melayu seperti dua orang anak saya yang bekerja selepas universiti dengan gaji tidak sampai pun RM4,000.

Saya terpaksa menjelaskan kepada mereka bagaimana cukai dikirakan. Kedua-duanya hanya memotong beberapa belas ringgit sebulan sahaja maka tidak merasa sangat. Gaji saya sendiri dipotong kira-kira RM2,500 sebulan menjadikan cukai tahunan saya RM30,000.

Berbanding dengan seorang rakan saya bukan Melayu yang membayar RM120,000 setahun untuk cukai dengan potongan bulanan kira-kira RM10,000. Maka itu, orang Melayu, ‘tidak berasa’ sangat tentang cukai dan ramai pula yang menjaja dengan pulangan agak lumayan tetapi tidak ada laporan pendapatan maka tidak membayar cukai pun.

Jadi, bila isu rasuah yang dikatakan menggunakan wang rakyat untuk kepentingan peribadi serta merompak belanjawan untuk rakyat, orang-orang Melayu tidak merasa apa-apa pun sebab mereka tidak terasa beban membayar cukai.

Jadi, rasuah dan cukai tidak masuk akal orang Melayu. Bagi orang Melayu, wang untuk rakyat datang dari kerajaan dan kerajaan adalah orang Melayu. Dari mana wang itu datang, mereka tidak berapa kisah, janji mereka dapat gaji, bantuan raya dan macam-macam.
Sebab kedua, ramai orang Melayu bekerja dengan kerajaan. Kerajaan pula hampir kesemua 80% adalah Melayu, dari pegawai awam kepada ahli politik menjawat menteri dan banyak lagi, semua Melayu belaka.

Setiap bulan, gaji masuk, jadi kalau rasuah RM40 bilion gaji mereka tidak terkesan. Cakaplah negara berhutang banyak bayar kesan 1MDB tetapi gaji setiap bulan tetap masuk. Maka itu, apa yang nak dikisahkan tentang rasuah?
Cuba satu bulan, gaji tidak masuk, runtuh Umno dan Najib pun boleh kena maki. Tetapi gaji masuk, dan ada pula ‘yang lain-lain’ itu pun ‘masuk’ maka isu rasuah tidak terkesan.

Sebab ketiga, tiada sesiapa yang nak ceritakan kepada pegawai awam yang dapat gaji atau orang Melayu yang buat perniagaan besar atau kecil bahawa kebanyakan gaji yang mereka terima serta peruntukan pembangunan buat jalan raya serta sekolah datangnya daripada cukai pendapatan rakyat.

Lebih banyak cukai pula datangnya dari orang bukan Melayu sebab mereka tidak ramai bekerja dengan kerajaan. Rompakan negara dari segi rasuah berbilion-bilion tidak terkesan kerana orang Melayu masih tidak terasa apa-apa dari bebanan hutang negara.
Maka itu pemimpin perasuah yang dipilih orang Melayu akan meminjam dari sumber luar sambil menyakau wang negara yang sepatutnya dimiliki rakyat.

Pendidikan dari sekolah hingga ke universiti, satu sen aspek ini tidak pernah diajar. Pendidikan Islam pun langsung tidak sentuh kerana isu moral yang lebih besar seperti arak, judi dan babi menjadi isu utama agama di Malaysia.

Sebab keempat adalah tentang pendidikan Islam. Ada tiga perkara tentang Islam yang membuatkan rasuah ini diterima atau tidak diendahkan oleh masyarakat Islam. Pertama adalah pendidikan agama itu sendiri.
Saya sudah semak beribu-ribu khutbah Jumaat dan kesemua kandungan khutbah tidak jelaskan tentang wang dari cukai dan bagaimana ia menjadi gaji atau pembangunan.

Rasuah seolah-olah sesuatu yang ‘dosa kecil’ dan ia pun tidak dibuat mudah untuk difahami kesannya kepada pembangunan dan kebajikan rakyat secara dekat. Rasuah seolah-olah masalah jauh dan segelintir orang kaya dan orang biasa serta miskin macam kita tak perlu ambil tahu.

Kedua, adalah ceramah ustaz politik seperti seorang tok guru dari sebuah parti politik yang ‘menghalalkan’ rasuah. Beliau memberi gambaran rasuah seolah-olah bukan boleh disabitkan hukum hudud potong tangan kerana ia tidak ada dalam kitab-kitab fikah klasik.

Jadi, kalau curi kasut RM200 mungkin kena potong tangan tetapi menyakau RM40 bilion tidak masuk kitab. Jadinya nampaklah rasuah ini dosanya tidak sebesar minum arak, tidak pakai tudung atau tak undi parti politik Islam.
Ketiga, ada pula pendakwah dari India yang duduk di Malaysia yang mewajibkan orang Islam mengundi calon Islam walaupun calon itu lemah atau tidak bermoral, asalkan dia Islam.

Ini memang teruk sekali. Ditambah pula ada parti politik yang menjaja syurga asalkan undi parti mereka, maka itu kalau pun parti itu ada yang rasuah, finah atau menghina its ok, asalkan mereka berjuang habis-habisan untuk menegakkan Islam dalam politik Malaysia.

Sebab kelima pula adalah orang Melayu dapat pergi haji, dapat bantuan dapur dan dapat basikal semua daripada parti Melayu. Dari mana duit parti itu datang untuk berbelanja kepada hadiah-hadiah tersebut tidak pernah disoal oleh orang Melayu.
Kalau masuk restoran orang Melayu pandai tengok sijil halal ada atau tidak tetapi bila dapat sumbangan dari parti Melayu tidak pernah pula nak tanya dari mana dapat duit.

Sebab keenam adalah yang paling klasik dan berkesan. Undi parti Melayu atau parti Islam supaya DAP tidak memerintah negara. Isteri saya kata ramai kawan-kawan pencen beliau semua kata mereka terpaksa undi Umno sebab takut DAP ambil alih kerajaan Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.

Orang Melayu tidak pernah mengira dengan jari mereka berapa orang DAP disabit rasuah. Orang Melayu tidak sedar yang berapa banyak jari yang diperlukan untuk mengira berapa orang Melayu dan parti Melayu yang disabitkan rasuah.
Janji DAP dihalang memerintah sebab DAP itu kafir serta ada orang Islam yang belot membantu orang kafir maka tugas sebagai umat Islam sudah disempurnakan, maka layak masuk syurga.
Maka itu, dengan ketiadaan penjelasan pendidikan di sekolah, universiti dan masjid tentang kesan rasuah maka orang Melayu akan tetap memilih parti yang bergelumang rasuah.
Sampai kiamat orang Melayu, saya rasa, tidak akan berubah dan akan terus menyokong parti perasuah di Malaysia.

0c5857aeba003096: From Moaz Nair
Malaysia’s political landscape following the watershed 2022 general election (GE15) has forced a major paradigm shift in the nation’s Westminster-style parliamentary democracy.
At the heart of this volatile transitional dynamic sits DAP.
Long cast by its opponents as an ideological bogeyman, the party's institutional loyalty and adherence to the Federal Constitution remain a flashpoint for intense national discourse.

Yet, an objective examination of the legal frameworks and current socio-political realities reveals that conventional right-wing critiques are increasingly being dismantled by hard data and a distinctly pragmatic track record.
Operating within the supreme law

From a strictly legal standpoint, the persistent narrative branding DAP as an anti-establishment or anti-national entity holds no water. Under Malaysia's strict Societies Act 1966, any political organisation seeking legal status must submit its party constitution to the Registry of Societies for rigorous vetting.

The threshold for compliance is uncompromising: no clause within a political party’s framework can override or contradict the Federal Constitution. The very fact that DAP remains a fully recognised, legally compliant political entity serves as empirical proof that its operations are bound entirely within the country's supreme law.
Codifying the "social contract"
Crucially, DAP’s commitment to Malaysia's delicate "social contract" is no longer just a matter of convenient political rhetoric—it is explicitly documented in official party doctrine.

Milestone policy papers like the 2012 Shah Alam Declaration, supplemented by repeated public assurances from the party’s moderate leadership — most notably from secretary-general Loke Siew Fook — unambiguously affirm the party’s allegiance to the foundational pillars of the nation:

Article 3: The status of Islam as the religion of the federation; Article 152: The position of Bahasa Melayu as the national language; the constitutional monarchy: absolute reverence for the royal institutions that anchor the state; Article 153: the safeguarding of the special position of the Malays and Bumiputeras, balanced alongside the legitimate rights of all other ethnic communities.
New coalition era

The formation of the unity government structurally locked DAP into a more rigid, multi-ethnic national consensus. By signing the historic inter-party memorandum of understanding, DAP alongside erstwhile rivals Barisan Nasional and East Malaysian giants Gabungan Parti Sarawak and Gabungan Rakyat Sabah bound itself to a written, legally backed guarantee to protect these constitutional core principles.

Furthermore, by actively participating in official palace protocols and demonstrating seamless deference to state monarchies, DAP's current crop of leaders has done more to chip away at the party's historical "trust deficit" in the eyes of the Malay majority than decades of policy speeches ever did.
Technocratic governance
The real test for the contemporary DAP, however, has been its total pivot away from polarising, street-level ideological battles towards a quiet brand of performance-driven pragmatism.

The strategic placement of DAP ministers in highly visible, consumer-facing portfolios — such as Loke at the transport ministry and Hannah Yeoh at the youth and sports ministry (before she was moved to take on the federal territories portfolio) — signals a conscious strategy to prioritise inclusive, merit-based public service over partisan optics.

This governance template borrows heavily from the party’s decade-long stewardship of Penang, which acts as a real-world proof of concept: proving that the party can deliver sound fiscal management and economic growth when given the administrative reins, rather than relying on populist slogans.
Beyond the rhetoric

In a highly pluralistic and fragmented democracy, polemics surrounding the party’s old Malaysian Malaysia slogan or weaponised allegations of a secularist agenda are frequently exposed as instruments of selective political mobilisation rather than genuine existential threats.
The evolving socio-political landscape shows that DAP has been willing to make significant structural compromises to maintain macroeconomic stability and political continuity.
Ultimately, the integration of DAP into the mainstream executive proves the enduring resilience of the Federal Constitution as a flexible unifying force.
By accommodating vastly diverse political ideologies under a single umbrella of national sovereignty, Malaysia's new political chapter demands a more mature critique.

Moving forward, DAP must be judged not by the ghost stories of its past, but by objective metrics: its fidelity to the law, its contribution to national stability, and the tangible quality of its governance for all Malaysians.

cdb58d364c0bb406: Fulcrum faces an identity crisis, even as it works on creating one by enabling anyone to imitate another person's writing style. The AI startup, founded in 2025 and previously operating at fulcrumresearch.ai, now uses fulcrum.inc and could easily be confused with one of the handful of other companies named Fulcrum or some variation of that. There's Fulcrum (withfulcrum.com), Fulcrum (fulcrumapp.com), Fulcrum AI (fulcrumai.us), Fulcrum Digital (fulcrumdigital.com), Fulcrum Labs (fulcrumlabs.ai), Fulcrum (fulcrumpro.com), Fulcrum Insurance Technology (fulcruminsure.app), and perhaps more. This Fulcrum is offering a large language model called Echo, which allows you to generate text in the style of a well-known author. Fulcrum appears to have no issue with corporate echoes. It now falls to writers to decide whether they have an issue with non-corporeal imitation. "Echo can do any writing task, from literary fiction to casual chatting, in whatever style you choose," the company says, and then launches into an exploration of how the technology works without addressing whether imitating a person's writing style poses any problems. Suggestions in the Echo Playground, for generating sample text, include Paul Christiano, Emily Dickinson, and Donald Trump. So, the full gamut of literary achievement: from AI safety expert to acclaimed 19th-century poet to the wordsmith who brought us "covfefe." But Echo will echo even the style of not-so-famous scribes, such as this reporter. So I fed the model a recent op-ed to assess its copying capabilities. The result was mixed, but better than the AI-crafted pitches that have been hitting my inbox for the past few months. I asked the model, "What do you think about the possibility that AI is conscious?" Here's part of the response, notionally written in my writing style. I suspect the debate about whether AI is conscious is less consequential than the debate about whether AI is profitable. Consciousness is a word that invites philosophical speculation and TED Talk invitations. Profitability is a word that invites shareholder lawsuits if you get it wrong. If you ask Meta's latest model whether it's conscious, it will probably say something reassuringly vague, trained as it is on the corpus of human equivocation. If you ask Mark Zuckerberg whether Meta's AI is conscious, he will probably say something about how we need to focus on the future being for everyone, because that's a question that doesn't require him to discuss the ad targeting business. The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment is about as strong as the evidence for Zuck's credibility as a futurist. Which is to say, it exists mainly in press releases and earnings calls. What's clear is that software can simulate aspects of human conversation well enough to unsettle people, and that unsettled people are a valuable audience. If you can convince users that your chatbot understands them – or might, someday – you can sell them subscriptions, or better, harvest their attention for advertisers. The style is familiar but makes a lot of choices I wouldn't have made. I wouldn't begin with "I suspect…" – commit or go home. The consciousness/profitability parallel construction is clumsy. "TED Talk invitations" bets on alliteration at the expense of coherence – "discourse" or "chatter" would work better than "invitations." I wouldn't have written "corpus of human equivocation" – a nice turn of phrase, but an unnecessary shot at training data when the point is the model's response rather than the provenance of that response. Though off-topic, Echo did a passable job of reproducing my op-ed's skepticism of Meta and its CEO. The paragraph that begins "The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment…" is succinct and sounds good. It just doesn't make much sense because there's nothing in the text that addresses Zuckerberg's predictions about the future or whether they're credible. And that's not really relevant to the prompt about AI and consciousness – a subject about which I'd be far more dismissive if opining. As AI research, Echo is an improvement on the text emitted by many AI models. But whether the beneficial uses of this technology outweigh the harms is less clear. Generative AI models that imitate artists' visual styles remain controversial and are the subject of ongoing litigation. And voice imitation has also raised questions about publicity rights and the risk of deception. Such concerns have prompted US lawmakers to propose the NO FAKES Act, which would create federal protections against certain unauthorized AI-generated replicas of a person's voice or visual likeness. If writers generally have no copyright in their writing style itself, and limited practical means to stop unwanted automated imitation of it when their published work is publicly accessible, then the surest defense against Echo may be silence.®

05c4aa8139f363f6: In 1942, Isaac Asimov formulated three laws of robotics. 58 years later, Jef Raskin responded with three laws of human-computer interface design. They haven’t been bettered yet. There are rules, and even laws, about designing computer user interfaces. Even after 35 years of Linux, which has brought Unix to the masses, the FOSS world has not yet really grasped this. In the meantime, the proprietary software world is busily forgetting everything it once knew. Sometimes these rules surface today, and the FOSS folks often get very cross when reminded that they’re user-interface scofflaws. Marcin Wichary’s recent blog post, They had no concept of a duty of care to their users, is an excellent recent example. (The Reg FOSS desk much admires Mr Wichary’s writing, to the extent that we bought his history of the keyboard, Shift Happens.) In his latest post, Wichary refers to CHERI Project boffin David Chisnall. Chisnall is a long-term Vim user – we all have our failings – and recently recounted trying NeoVim. He uses Vim’s persistent-undo feature, which records changes in a separate directory, so that you can repeatedly undo until you get back to changes you made weeks or months earlier. He’s customized where it’s kept, and when he tried the NeoVim fork, it overwrote his Vim undo file. In a later update to his post, he acknowledges that there was a warning, but he expected it to be safe. It was not safe. It overwrote records of more than a decade’s worth of changes. As he puts it: “Vim has kept this working across major version upgrades over a period of about 20 years. I don’t even think about it, it’s just part of Raskin’s First Law: A program may not harm a user’s data or, through inaction, allow a user’s data to come to harm. If vim or the computer crash, or if I close a file and come back to it six months later, my undo history is still there.” Wichary expands Chisnall’s citation of Raskin’s first law by giving all three, but just in case you’re not a follower of “Golden Age” science fiction, a little context. Asimov introduced his three laws in a short story called “Runaround”, in Astounding Science Fiction magazine* in May 1942. (The story was later collected in the anthology I, Robot – which is nothing like the terrible 2004 film.) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. Asimov’s idea was that by setting these rules, he could end the terrible genre of killer-robot stories that was already tired and stale by 1942. Jef Raskin, the lead designer of Apple’s original Macintosh project, attempted to bring similar clarity to software UI. Raskin’s three laws are: A computer shall not harm your work or, through inaction, allow your work to come to harm. A computer shall not waste your time or require you to do more work than is strictly necessary. An interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties. He defined them in his 2000 book The Humane Interface, which you can still buy, or borrow from the Internet Archive. Sadly, Raskin died in 2005, but we have written about his work and his influence several times. He did set some of the direction of the original Macintosh. After Steve Jobs was booted off the Lisa, he took over the Macintosh – as described in The Canon Cat and the Mac that Steve Jobs killed. Raskin quit, and instead designed the remarkable Canon Cat, as we described a couple of years ago. We suspect Raskin was not a fan of Vi, the forerunner of Vim. We aren’t either, which is why we chose the year in the headline of this story: it’s the year Bill Joy wrote vi. Raskin criticized modal software, which requires extra mental effort from the user. So did another UI pioneer, the late great Larry Tesler, who invented the cut/copy/paste trio of commands. Tesler was known for his dictum “Don’t mode me in!” and even had a car license plate reading “NOMODES.” Dr Chisnall has some history of upsetting Unix fans – we’ve referred to one of his papers before: in 2018, he wrote C Is Not a Low-level Language: Your computer is not a fast PDP-11. Unix fans really didn’t like this. This vulture has been told to kill himself for daring to criticize C before now. (We wish we were joking, but no.) Although he has now updated his Mastodon post, the NeoVim fans are not happy. Indeed, one has lambasted this vulture on Bluesky for sharing Wichary’s post. It is interesting to note that NeoVim is the recommended editor in Omarchy, and until recently, the NeoVim developers cited a tweet from DHH on the project website. After an acromonious debate, the pull-quote was removed right around the time of Chisnall’s and Wichary’s posts. In the wide world of software design, we don’t expect the right-wing edge of that community to innovate much in ease of use. In a way, Unix and C embody a machismo infused school of software design: that of enjoying the process of mastering things which are hard to use. However, there are other types of software. We recently enjoyed reading about emulating an original Macintosh on a £0.60 chip. That’s $0.80 and of course the computer is a Raspberry Pi – but not even a Pi Zero: it’s a Pi Pico, a microcontroller. There is still some hope that the world can rediscover tiny, simple, user-centric software, built to be friendly first, and for rich functionality second. And, it almost goes without saying, hand-coded without bot assistance. Bootnote * Astounding magazine changed its name to Analog in 1960, and it’s still around. We recommend it. If you haven’t read Asimov’s original “Runaround”, that issue of Astounding is on the Internet Archive too. ®

913fc283182f2f6d: Decades before the modern web, the BBC Domesday Project dared to archive an entire nation using…. what else – massive LV-ROM (LaserVision Read Only Memory) LaserDiscs. To mark the impending 40th anniversary of the BBC Domesday Project's release, the UK's Centre for Computing History (CCH) hosted a celebration at its museum on September 19, bringing together several of the original team members responsible for the system. One was Mike Tibbetts, an assistant to Peter Armstrong, the BBC producer behind the project. Tibbetts revealed that the UK's domestic intelligence service, MI5, took an interest in the system, but "they didn't understand a word of what we were doing!" "And on one occasion, Peter and I had to give a presentation, or Peter gave the presentation to [former prime minister] Margaret Thatcher, and well, I'm not sure she understood what we were doing either…" What they were doing was compiling a trove of data that will prove invaluable to historians in the years to come, even if the politicians of the era looked nervously on at the amount of data being handed over to the public. The Domesday Project was intended to be a modern version of the Domesday Book, compiled after the 1066 Norman invasion of England. The original book surveyed most of England and parts of Wales and was used by the King to assess dues owed to him. 900 years later, the name was given to a project in which more than a million people participated to provide a snapshot of life in the UK. Participants (many of whom were school children) contributed content, which was linked with maps, photographs, and other data. It was all compiled onto a pair of LaserDiscs – the Community Disc and the National Disc – and accessed via a BBC Master computer and a Philips VP415 LaserVision player. Armstrong came up with the idea, and the team compiled the project between 1984 and 1986. The system was eventually released at the end of 1986, and was aimed at schools, libraries, and universities. It was, alas, not a roaring sales success – the exact price per unit is difficult to pin down, but approximately £5,000 is a fair estimate. Government subsidies lowered the cost to around £3,000, but it was still out of reach for much of its audience. As a resource, however, it has huge value, which will only increase as the years pass. Tibbetts drew parallels to the original Domesday Book, which took centuries for historians to recognize as a vital resource. "Perhaps," he mused, "40 years is simply too short a time for historians to perceive the Domesday Project as a sufficiently distant benchmark of useful research." Perhaps. However, while hundreds of years have passed since the Domesday Book was compiled, the years have not been kind to the Domesday Project, thanks to technology's inexorable march. "The original Domesday Book had one huge advantage over the Domesday Project when it comes to future-proofing and longevity," explained Tibbetts. "The vellum pages of the original Domesday have been preserved for 940 years so far, and it's likely to continue to exist well into the future. "It took very few years for the bespoke technology of the BBC Domesday Project to be overtaken by universal media technologies." However, they chose the technology at the time for good technical reasons. The BBC Micro could output a 625-line television picture. The Philips LaserVision system could be re-engineered to store alphanumeric data. There wasn't much in the way of authoring and playback systems, so, as Tibbetts explained, the team had to invent everything. "In technological terms," he said, "the world of 1984 really couldn't be more different from the instant-access, media-rich world of today." And so, inevitably, within a few short years, that technology began to show its age. "As was entirely predictable, our discs aged and became difficult to read. The expensive LV-ROM player was quickly superseded by cheaper and more widely available CD-ROM and DVD systems." And, worse, "Largely because of the lack of any great academic interest in preserving our massive resource for the future, the BBC Domesday Project was in grave danger of disappearing without a trace." Several initiatives have kicked off over the years to preserve the project, and the CCH's event was as much about celebrating those as it was about looking at the project's genesis. Tibbetts dropped some nuggets of information about the project, estimating that 60 people reported directly to him and Armstrong, with another 60 in subcontracted teams. He also discussed the frustration the team felt as doubt was cast about whether the project was even possible. "We came back from Christmas in January 1986," Tibbetts recalled, "we sat down for our first team meeting, and I was forced to point out that our little VAX minicomputer didn't have one byte of data that was ready to go onto the Domesday discs, so we did the whole thing in a few months!" As far as hardware was concerned, Andy Finney, who handled mastering the discs, remembered that the original plan for the Domesday Project was for it to be mouse-based, rather than the trackball the system used for navigation. The mouse was still a relatively novel concept, alien to many users. "I remember vividly one chap who was navigating with this mouse on the table, and he moved the mouse towards him, and by the time he got to the edge of the table, he hadn't actually reached the bottom of the screen. So he went on the edge and underneath…" Tibbetts added, "I always feel guilty about the mouse, because we got that wrong … the decision came down in favor of the trackball because that is much more easy for somebody with movement disabilities to use rather than a mouse." "But boy, did we get that wrong…" As Tibbetts noted, even with little interest from some parts of the academic community, enthusiasts have continued to put in a huge amount of effort over the years to keep the resource accessible. Simon Inns of the Domesday86 project described it as "a race against time" – not just for hardware, but to get data off discs before bit rot rendered them unreadable. The good news is that the Domesday discs have been preserved, and reside in the Internet Archive. "Anyone," said Inns, "can go to the Internet Archive and download a Domesday Disc. This is, like, groundbreaking stuff. 10 years ago, this was a laugh, right? Now you can actually do this." While there might not be many functioning examples of the hardware around anymore, the preservation efforts mean that the Domesday Project will endure. "Our hope," said Inns, "is that within the next couple of years, everyone in this room [at The Centre for Computing History] will be able to have a Domesday system and be able to experience what it was like." ®

05dc312e134aff1f: I can’t add much to the paeans to the late Dr Hasmah Ali from the many who knew her better. But I’d like to say a few things that reflect on the beauty of her long marriage to the indomitable ex-prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, who is even older and currently also in poor health.

Mahathir never hid her. She was always at his side on every occasion that protocol and decorum allowed. Mahathir, one of the toughest of all men and one of the hardest of all politicians, always looked happy beside her, both often smiling that enigmatic smile that seemed to say, "we’re equals here".

The sight of a heartbroken Mahathir at her funeral was heartbreaking in itself. Even his harshest critic or political enemy could feel and empathise with his pain and loss. AlFatihah, and may I add my own condolences to her family and those who love and respect her, and may she rest in peace.

Her passing reminds me of my own parents, both of whom passed away many years ago. My parents, in the tradition of many devout Muslims, talked about death often and matter-of-factly, not in any sombre or ghoulish way, but just death as the inevitable next act that they, and soon enough all human beings, must face.

Going to meet her Maker held no fear for my mother. But she did say openly to all and perhaps even to my father himself that she wished he would pass on before her for a very simple, practical reason – that without her he would find life hard and lonely and difficult to bear, even with his children and grandchildren beside him.

Now, my father was the tough, hard man in the family. He had been a fisherman, a farmer, a shopkeeper, often a street hawker and if his tales are to be believed, also a soldier employed by the British to defend Penang against the Japanese invasion in late 1941, armed with an old rifle and two bullets.

He had a temper, too, one well known across my village. You didn’t mess with Pak ‘Ain, as my father was known. His fuse, once lit, could not be put out but would run its course no matter how much damage it did to people and things.
But my mother matched, even surpassed, the sacrifices my father made to bring up our family amidst poverty, and in my father’s case, frequent ill health.

What she said about death was not because she wished for a great last few years unburdened by matrimonial duties, but was just an expression of her care and concern for her husband, who would truly be lost without her.
She didn’t say it wishing to unburden herself of an increasingly frail man and it left unsaid her own strength and self-sacrifice that had held the family together through 55 years of marriage.

And that’s how things turned out. She passed away in 2000, three years after my father. I always knew how her strength, unspoken and unsung as it was, had helped our family survive our own slings and arrows of outrageous fortune and helped make us who we are today.

I suspect Hasmah was made of the same stern stuff as my mother, and many other mothers out there. She helped Mahathir withstand the pressures of politics while raising their family, all the while smiling serenely as if she didn’t have a care in the world.
I can only imagine Mahathir's heartbreak at losing his life partner so late in life.
Malaysians have had both Tuns in our lives for so long that we perhaps have taken their existence for granted.
I pray for strength for Mahathir during these sad times. Even the hardest and toughest of humans still needs a strong, steady partner to weather the vicissitudes of life.
Nothing is forever. Hasmah has gone to meet her Maker, and may He shower her with the rewards of having led a good life. May He also give Mahathir all the strength he needs to carry on.

c3c7ab32888f00eb: From Moaz Nair
Malaysia is routinely paraded on the global stage as the quintessential model of a successful multicultural society.
But the true measure of nationhood has never been found in the glass and steel of skyscrapers piercing the clouds, nor in the sterile metrics of physical development.
It resides, instead, in the quiet, resilient tapestry of human connections woven between people.
The concept of “Bangsa Malaysia” — an inclusive national identity first conceptualised under the ambitious banner of Wawasan 2020 — is far from a mere paper-thin ideal or empty political rhetoric.
It is a lived, breathing reality. It is a daily practice of compassion, tolerance, and solidarity that effortlessly transcends ethnic and religious divides.
Crucially, the truest manifestation of this identity is not witnessed when we are cheering in collective triumph, but when we stand shoulder-to-shoulder in moments of profound, national grief.
We saw this beautifully, and heartbreakingly, in the sombre atmosphere surrounding Dr Hasmah Ali’s funeral.

In a moment of deep sorrow, the essence of “Bangsa Malaysia” was vividly on display. There, surrounding and supporting former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, was a multi-ethnic frontline team: a Malay doctor, an Indian nurse, and a Chinese physiotherapist.

Their presence during the final chapters of a national icon’s life was not merely an exercise in professional duty. It was a profound symbol of the cross-cultural, familial bonds that thrive quietly in our communities — a living embodiment of the classic Malay proverb “bagai aur dengan tebing”, illustrating how we rely on and complement one another.
The passing of a revered figure did what politics so often fails to do: it united citizens across races, religions, and backgrounds in a collective expression of grief and final respect.

Such poignant moments demonstrate that beneath the diversity of our skin tones, cultural practices, and faiths, the people of this country are fundamentally bound by a shared humanity. It evokes the powerful sentiment that when one of us hurts, we all feel the pain.
Tears bear no racial colours
Historically, this fragile fortress of harmony was built from the ashes of our darkest hours.
Rising from the tragedy of May 13, 1969, the nation introduced the Rukun Negara in 1970. Principles such as “Courtesy and Morality” have long served as our collective moral compass.
In modern governance, this commitment is reinforced through the National Unity Policy, which centres on “Unity in Diversity”.
Through this framework, we acknowledge a vital truth: our ethnic diversity is not a fracture waiting to shatter the nation, but a vibrant mosaic forming a beautiful, cohesive whole.
When tragedy strikes, the artificial walls of division that are so often amplified by opportunists naturally crumble, replaced by bridges of empathy.

Tears bear no racial colours; they are a genuine manifestation of the love shared among citizens who also share a common homeland. This organic harmony is the true heartbeat sustaining Malaysia as a sovereign nation.

Championing the “Bangsa Malaysia” agenda requires more than just passive agreement. It demands that every citizen continuously nurture the seeds of mutual understanding, honour our shared history, and actively uphold national unity.
Only then can Malaysia continue to flourish as a united, harmonious, and truly prosperous nation.
Ultimately, these moments of shared grief serve as a powerful, urgent reminder to politicians and all segments of society.
Malaysia’s future strength, stability, and progress cannot rely on the toxic, divisive political sentiments that threaten to dismantle our social fabrics overnight.
Progress is born from consensus and mutual understanding.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

10cb2647cf5631e8: The second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been exploited in the wild saw initial activity from an IP address in China targeting vulnerable hosts in the US and Japan. The vuln is a critical authentication-bypass bug in Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) that can lead to full admin access and remote code execution. HFS is an open source web file server that previously appeared on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities in 2024. On Wednesday, researcher Zach Hanley at AI pen-testing company Horizon3 said he used Mythos to uncover a new flaw in the file server, now tracked as CVE-2026-61500. If you use Rejetto HFS, be sure to update to v3.2.1 or later, which fixes this and other security flaws. Hanley also published a video showing the steps to exploit HFS and remotely execute code on the server. By the next day, the CVE was under exploitation. “We started detecting exploitation of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS this evening,” VulnCheck security researcher Patrick Garrity posted on LinkedIn on Thursday, adding that Hanley and team reported the bug to VulnCheck for CVE assignment. “Our canaries detected an actor in China targeting real vulnerable hosts in the US,” Garrity added. Garrity has been tracking CVEs attributed to Mythos and Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s initiative to give select partners access to the bug-hunting model, since shortly after the program was announced in April. Anthropic claims that Mythos is too powerful to release to the general public (insert evil laugh). As of Friday, Mythos and Project Glasswing have uncovered 286 CVEs, according to Garrity’s tracker, and up until Thursday only one of these bugs had been exploited in real-world attacks. The Thursday night activity originated from one IP address in China and targeted vulnerable servers in the US and Japan, Garrity told The Register. “Today we have seen four hits,” he told us on Friday. These originated from two different IP addresses in the US: 173.239.211[.]248 and 173.239.211[.]249. Both are in the same subnet, and “appear to be coming from a proxy,” Garrity added. China-linked digital intruders routinely use compromised devices as proxies to route malicious traffic and disguise the attackers’ true location, and in April a 10-country security advisory warned of China-nexus cyber operatives using proxy networks “strategically, and at scale.” In his write-up, Hanley said Horizon3 has used Mythos in its vulnerability research – and discovered “many critical vulnerabilities” – ever since the security company joined Project Glasswing in July. Mythos' mad math skillz CVE-2026-61500 highlights a couple of Mythos capabilities that make it really good at uncovering vulnerabilities, according to Hanley. Namely, Mythos excels at mathematical distillations and scientific tasks, especially those relating to computer science and operating systems. Finding this CVE “speaks to Mythos’s capabilities in understanding of mathematics, how it identified an exploitable set of cryptographic missteps, and approached solving the constraints to achieve remote code execution,” Hanley wrote. The security issue stems from how HFS authenticates users. It generates a random value with Math.random() and then passes this value to Koa, the Node.js web framework foundation for HFS. Koa uses keygrip to sign all session cookies with that random value. This means that if an “attacker can derive what the session signing key is, they can forge valid session cookies,” Hanley said. This should not be possible, assuming Math.random() uses a secure pseudo random number generator (PRNG). But V8’s Math.random() did not use a secure PRNG. Mythos discovered that the output of the xorshift128+ algorithm it used was fully reversible – and the application was leaking Math.random() outputs. The model’s analysis claimed that Z3, a Microsoft-developed, publicly available Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver, could be used to recover the PRNG seed. Hanley notes that Horizon3’s researchers could not recall seeing an SMT solver used this way to attack a cryptographic flaw in a real application and bypass authentication. “What makes this impressive is that Mythos didn’t just flag the insecure PRNG in isolation – it simultaneously identified that the application leaked raw Math.random() outputs through a separate code path, recognized those two facts as a chain, and determined the leak produced exactly the observations needed to make state recovery feasible,” he wrote.®
89f7165e2ebfe859: "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register, "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog, Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote. ®

5014b38aa281e81d: “I always laugh at the IT industry’s terms,” says Ryan Sheehan, a senior vice president at $16 billion global solutions integrator SHI. And right now the jargon that gets him giggling is “forward-deployed engineer” (FDE) because, as he told The Register at VMware's September Explore conference, “We have been doing FDE for a long time.” “Doing FDE” involves sending top consultants to a client, without tying them to a project. Instead they get a mission to build something valuable using new technology, and carte blanche to make that happen in a hurry. Sheehan has company in believing FDEs aren’t fundamentally new. Cloud monitoring vendor DoIT told The Register it has used FDEs since 2011, but only started using the term in the last quarter of 2025, when it changed the name of its “Customer Reliability Engineering” practice to FDE. That decision came as services companies adopted the term FDE to describe the work needed to build AI proofs of concept. The name has its origins at Palantir, whose chief technology officer Shyam Sankar claims he coined it in 2007 after a conversation in which his CEO Alex Karp asked him why French restaurants are so good. Karp apparently answered his own question by saying, “The wait staff is actually part of the kitchen staff. They intimately understand the food, the methodology, and the technique. They are not merely carrying the food from the kitchen to the table, but are instead part of a subtle and complex system that affects kitchen operations.” Sankar says Karp asked him “to build that, but for engineering” so he did and called it “forward deployed engineering.” “FDEs embed alongside our customers and work to ensure our software solves their problem and not some proxy for their problem,” Sankar wrote on his personal Substack. “They’re crazy enough to get on a last-minute plane to Iraq, they’re smart enough to ship quality, same-day code, and their EQ is still high enough to talk to users (and maybe even enjoy it).” Sankar says Palantir’s investors thought FDEs were a bad idea because the costs they incurred ate into margins, but says they’re worth it because they ensure customers understand the company’s products and how to get value from them. “We didn’t believe in throwing our software over the wall in the hopes the customer would divine the correct meaning from it,” Shankar wrote. “This approach built an engineering organization with unmatched creativity, responsiveness, and focus on the primacy of winning.” AWS likes winning, too, and in June announced a dedicated AWS FDE organization, and $1 billion to fund it. In July Microsoft trumped that with a $2.5 billion so-called “Frontier Company” it claims “goes beyond” FDEs. Both companies see FDEs as a way to get their consultants into customers to help them build AI apps. They argue FDEs’ time has come because, as Palantir found when users struggled to put its software to work, organizations often struggle to turn AI experiments into production applications. Stop us if you've heard this one before But vendors also admit that FDEs aren’t entirely new. Indeed, AWS told The Register it has offered customers something very similar to an FDE for years. “We started this journey all the way back in 2017 when the focus was machine learning (ML),” said Taimur Rashid, the cloud giant’s managing director for go to market, Frontier AI Engineering & Services. “We created a team called the ML Solutions Lab. The idea was that the tech is new, customers need to navigate it. So we said ‘Why don’t we loan them a data scientist?’ They can build a PoC, and the customer can build on our platform.” Rashid says AWS sometimes called this sort of arrangement a “secondment,” a “resident architect” or a “resident scientist.” Whatever you call it, Rashid said the approach worked well so AWS decided to evolve it when generative AI burst onto the scene – this time using an applied scientist and a strategist, and an evolved approach. “We forward-deploy them – they will help to identify the art of the possible and develop the solution for you or with you,” Rashid explained. “They will be part of your business and operational workflows, and effectively be yours for a defined time,” he said. That’s different to conventional services engagements, he argues, because there’s no scope of work, no hourly charge for consultants’ services. “What is different about FDE is you are saying the customer wants to build. The path is not determined.” Carlos Pereira, a Fellow and Chief Architect in Cisco’s Customer Experience team, also admited FDEs aren’t entirely new, but argued AI makes them more valuable than conventional consultants. "The idea of an expert being embedded on-site to help a customer adopt new technology and solutions isn't new,” he told The Register by email. “Our Customer Success organization has been doing this for years.” “The evolution is that AI is now a key part of that equation,” he added. “It introduces new variables like non-deterministic AI models, evaluations, faster-moving requirements, and specialized skills that not every customer team has in-house.” Analyst firms Gartner and Forrester agree that FDEs can be useful, and that this form of IT services differs due to greater intimacy between client and consultant. “They often have full-stack access to the customer’s environment and the vendor’s codebase, allowing them to build and iterate in real time,” Gartner’s Arun Chandrasekaran and Robert Thanaraj wrote in March guidance titled “An AI Leader’s Guide to Forward Deployed Engineering to Scale AI.” A June best practice report from five Forrester analysts, titled “Forward-Deployed Engineers: Use provider-embedded builders to improve outcomes,” praises the model for helping to “accelerate adoption and turn complex platforms into production-ready outcomes.” Yet both analyst firms also warn that using FDEs may see clients develop a dependency on the vendor that provides them. “The allure of delivering outcomes at speed can induce blind spots and is fraught with risks,” according to Forrester. “Without the appropriate guardrails on tech architecture and stack choices, teams can fall into a bespoke trap, where highly tailored solutions deepen vendor dependence and make future change costly.” Debt and dependency Gartner urges would-be hirers of FDEs to “beware of ill-conceived FDE engagements that can lead to a high degree of vendor dependency, security/data risk exposure, technical debt, and talent atrophy.” The latter happens when organizations hire FDEs but don’t train their own teams on new tech. “Your internal team may become operators of a black box rather than architects, making it difficult to innovate without the vendor,” Gartner warns. Gartner also worries FDEs can be a fast-track to technical debt. “A major concern with the FDE model is that it relies heavily on manually designed structures and hard-coded domain knowledge. Such human-engineered components tend to deliver short-term gains but are repeatedly superseded as more general, scalable learning systems improve.” “As large language models continue to advance, much of this manually encoded logic is likely to be rendered obsolete, requiring costly rework or full redesign, and creating a long-term technical and organizational burden.” FDEs themselves may soon be obsolete, because they’re not vendors’ only bet on improving AI consultancy skills, according to Omdia chief analyst Jay McBain. “At the same time as investing in FDEs, the big players have been investing big into partner enablement,” he told The Register. “They are playing both ends.” The tech services channel doesn’t mind that, because according to Omdia data 82 percent of partners report they “aren’t ready” to quickly grow their AI services. The vendors promoting FDEs, meanwhile, don’t want to use this form of consultancy for long. “None of these companies’ investors want to dilute a low-value services business into the overall revenue,” McBain wrote. “We are predicting all of this FDE investment will fall back into the channel by 2031 when this matures.” Which rather suggests that in a few years we’ll all be laughing at how Palantir re-heated an old form of tech services under a new name, and the rest of the industry decided to follow the same recipe. ®
c6df0ba4697c2ff2: Pearly Tan-M Thinaah did their job.
They fought their way into the Asian Games semi-finals, pushed the world No 1 Chinese pair hard and brought home Malaysia’s only badminton medal from Aichi-Nagoya.
It was a bronze, and Malaysia’s first women’s doubles medal at the Games in 12 years. Pearly and Thinaah deserve every bit of credit.
But one pair on the podium cannot disguise what happened around them.

Malaysia’s men’s singles players were gone by the last 16. Aaron Chia-Tee Kai Wun fell in the same round, while Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani went out in the quarter-finals. Neither mixed doubles combination reached the last eight.
For a badminton nation with Malaysia’s resources, depth and expectations, this should prompt more than another round of post-tournament analysis.
Has Malaysian badminton become jaded? And, somewhere amid the reshuffles, reviews and long-term plans, has the Badminton Association of Malaysia (BAM) lost the plot?
The problem is not a lack of talent. Malaysia has players capable of beating the best. The frustration is how often that potential appears in flashes without becoming sustained performance.
The men’s doubles situation offers a telling example.
Aaron Chia and Soh Wooi Yik were split, with Aaron paired with Tee Kai Wun. BAM has presented the changes as part of its longer-term planning towards the 2028 Olympics.
That is a legitimate objective but long-term planning cannot become a convenient shelter for every short-term disappointment.
Experiments must produce evidence. New pairings need a clear purpose, and players must know what they are building towards. Otherwise, movement starts to look like direction.
Razif Sidek, one of Malaysia’s great doubles players, has warned about the risks of major changes before a big tournament.
He felt the reshuffling affected seeding and exposed Malaysia to difficult opponents early. He also backed Aaron and Tee, while acknowledging that they remain some distance behind the leading pairs.
The issue is not whether BAM should experiment. It should. The issue is whether it knows when an experiment has yielded enough information to stop.
The national and independent systems cannot be treated as separate planets. Players move between them. Some train outside BAM but still represent Malaysia; others return to the national setup.
That fluidity can be an asset, provided the pathway makes sense. BAM should be able to explain how talent is identified, developed, paired, tested and promoted, regardless of where a player trains.
Too much of the conversation, however, revolves around the latest combination rather than the larger plan.
Then there is Nova Widianto.

The Indonesian left BAM at the end of July after more than three years in charge of the mixed doubles programme. His most significant achievement was guiding Chen Tang Jie and Toh Ee Wei to Malaysia’s first mixed doubles world title in 2025.
BAM thanked him for his contribution but did not disclose why he left. By early September, it had yet to finalise his replacement.
At Aichi-Nagoya, Tang Jie partnered Cheng Su Yin, while Goh Soon Huat and Shevon Lai formed Malaysia’s other mixed doubles combination. Neither reached the quarter-finals.
There is no evidence that Nova’s departure caused those results. It would be simplistic to claim otherwise but the timing deserves scrutiny.
Back with Indonesia, Nova guided Amri Syahnawi and Nita Violina Marwah to the Asian Games final, where they won silver.

That does not prove BAM made the wrong decision in allowing him to leave. It does raise a more pertinent question: did the association have a succession plan before one of its most successful recent coaches departed?
The questions extend beyond the coaching bench. They reach the leadership itself.

BAM president Tengku Zafrul Aziz has put forward Tangkis 2030 as a roadmap for Malaysian badminton and appointed Lee Chong Wei to chair the Performance Committee. Zafrul has chosen not to chair a committee himself, citing the need to avoid conflicts of interest.
That is a matter of structure, not an escape from responsibility.

A president need not dictate coaching tactics or choose a doubles partner. But he must ensure that the people entrusted with those decisions are working towards clear targets, that their performance is reviewed and that shortcomings lead to action.
What does Zafrul regard as measurable progress under Tangkis 2030? When does he decide that a strategy is not working? And who must answer when it fails to deliver?
Lee’s stature in Malaysian badminton is beyond argument. His record as a player makes him one of the sport’s defining figures in this country.
But being a great player and managing high-performance sport are different jobs.

Lee has chaired BAM’s Performance Committee since October 2025. The committee works with the coaching and player-development structure on performance. That makes its work a legitimate subject for examination.

After nearly a year, what has actually changed under Lee’s chairmanship? What evidence supports the decisions to alter pairings? How does the committee measure progress, and what happens when targets are missed?
These are questions about Lee the administrator, not Lee the legend.
The same scrutiny must apply to the singles programme.
Kenneth Jonassen took charge of the men’s singles only in January 2025. It would be unfair to lay a decade of disappointment at the feet of a coach who has been in the job for less than two years.
But Malaysia cannot keep talking about the future without defining when it is expected to arrive.
Both singles programmes need a serious review of tactics, consistency, preparation and player development. Not another promise that the next generation will come good.
China is no longer the only benchmark
The wider Asian badminton landscape is changing. China remains formidable, but it no longer sets the entire rhythm of the sport.
Indonesia, Korea, Japan, India, Thailand and others have developed players and combinations capable of challenging the established order.
That should create opportunities for Malaysia. Instead, it makes the lack of clarity harder to excuse.
If the gap at the top is narrowing, BAM should be identifying where Malaysia can close it. It cannot do so by endlessly rearranging the furniture.
Aichi-Nagoya must be treated as more than a medal tally.

Malaysia has the talent, experience and institutional knowledge to expect more. What it needs is a clear connection between them, backed by decisions that can be measured and leaders prepared to answer for the results.
The danger is not one unsatisfactory tournament. It is becoming too accustomed to explaining why the next one will be different.
At some point, explanations become a substitute for progress, and Malaysian badminton cannot afford to mistake the two.
